questions.question: I have no hosts at all, just aspects that set one custom class. Can I use den as a library to collect that class from an aspect and evaluate it myself?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Yes — that's exactly the documented "Den as a library" case, and hosts are entirely optional.

**The call you want:**

```nix
# den.aspects.my-aspect sets your custom class:
# den.aspects.my-aspect = { myclass = { ... }; };

module = den.lib.aspects.resolve "myclass" den.aspects.my-aspect;
# → { imports = [ <your class's modules> ... ]; }

# then evaluate it yourself, with any module system:
app = lib.evalModules { modules = [ module ]; };
```

`den.lib.aspects.resolve "<class>" <aspect>` walks the aspect tree (following `includes`, dispatching parametric aspects) and collects the content of that one class. It returns `{ imports = [ ... ]; }` — plain NixOS-style modules — and it's up to you what module system evaluates them (`lib.evalModules`, nvf's `neovimConfiguration`, Terranix, …). Nothing in the library layer touches `den.hosts`/`den.homes`; those are the optional framework layer on top.

**How I know:**

- `den.lib.aspects.resolve = fxResolveTree` in `nix/lib/aspects/default.nix` — the signature is `class: resolved: …`, a class name plus an aspect, no entity argument.
- `nix/lib/aspects/fx/resolve.nix`: `fxResolve = mkPipeline: args: { inherit (fxResolveFull mkPipeline args) imports; }`, with the comment that it "protects deferredModule consumers that assert resolve's output is exactly `{ imports = …; }`".
- The docs' **Library vs Framework** page: "Den's core (`nix/default.nix`) is domain-agnostic. `den.lib` exposes the resolution pipeline (`aspects.resolve`/`aspects.resolveImports`)… nothing here assumes NixOS, Darwin, or Home Manager", and under *When to use what*: "**Library only:** you have a custom Nix module system (Terranix, NixVim, system-manager) and want parametric aspect dispatch without Den's host/user/home framework."
- A shipped zero-hosts example: the `nvf-standalone` template (`templates/nvf-standalone/modules/nvf-integration.nix`) — aspects set a custom `vim` class, `den.lib.aspects.resolve "nvf" aspect` hands the result to `inputs.nvf.lib.neovimConfiguration { modules = [ … ]; }`, i.e. evaluated by nvf's own module system. No hosts anywhere in that flow.

**Two notes for your setup:**

1. If your aspect is parametric (a function of context, e.g. `{ mine }: …`), you supply the context yourself — in a no-hosts setup it's just any attrset you choose. The nvf template does `den.lib.parametric.fixedTo ctx { includes = [ … ]; }` and callers pass e.g. `{ mine = true }`. (The docs list the older `den.lib.parametric` helpers as deprecated in favor of automatic dispatch, but the current template still uses this pattern, so it works.)
2. `den.lib.aspects.resolveImports` is a variant that skips entity instantiation (phases 1–3 only) — useful if you're nesting resolutions and don't want the instantiate machinery.","confidence":0.85,"gaps":["Source was read via raw.githubusercontent.com (clone unavailable in this environment) on the main branch, not a pinned rev","Did not evaluate the nvf-standalone template's my-neovim output end-to-end to confirm the whole chain evaluates in the sandbox","Your specific aspect/custom-class setup was not evaluated"],"escalate_forced":"no"}

questions.question: A den quirk whose values depend on `config` works with `pipe.transform` when consumed from another host, but on the same host the transformed value is wrong. Is that a bug?

function.name: reply

{"answer":"The asymmetry is by design, but the value divergence you're seeing is in a part of den the maintainers explicitly flag as unfinished — so: not an accidental regression, and a genuinely wrong same-host value is reportable against the documented contract.

**How the two paths work** (denful/den, main; verified in source):
- A config-dependent quirk value (a fn reading `config`/`osConfig`/`pkgs`) is not resolved at pipe assembly. `assemble-pipes.nix` (`markConfigThunks`) turns it into a `__configThunk` marker, and `deferredStage` defers any transform stage over it — your `pipe.transform` becomes `__post`, applied *after* resolution.
- **Cross-host** (`pipe.collect`/`pipe.broadcast`): the thunk is resolved eagerly at assembly time against `hostConfigs.${sourceScopeId}` — the producer's precomputed, fully instantiated config (the B′ pass in `resolve.nix`). PR #625 (merged Jul 2026) made this path work end-to-end (test `bprime-basedrain-crosshost`) — matches your "works from another host".

questions.question: Does using den make Nix evaluation of my NixOS systems slower than wiring nixosSystem by hand?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**Short answer: no meaningful slowdown — the heavy part is identical.** den does not replace `nixosSystem`; for each NixOS host it calls exactly the same nixpkgs function you'd wire by hand. What den adds is a bounded pre-pass in front of it.

What I verified in den's source (`sini/den` @ `2589d73`, main, Jun 15 2026):

1. **Final eval is stock `lib.nixosSystem`.** In `nix/lib/entities/host.nix`, the host's `instantiate` option defaults to `inputs.nixpkgs.lib.nixosSystem` (for `class = "nixos"`), and `intoAttr` defaults to `[ "nixosConfigurations" name ]`. The docs (`reference/output.mdx`) show the same: "For each host in `den.hosts`, Den calls `host.instantiate { modules = [ host.mainModule … ]; }`" — overridable, e.g. to `nixos-unstable.lib.nixosSystem`.

2. **One resolve per entity, then the standard call.** In `nix/lib/entities/_types.nix`, `__resolveResult` is `den.lib.aspects.resolveWithPaths config.class config.resolved`, declared as a module option "so the module fixpoint memoizes it — every consumer (mainModule, __pathSetByScope) reads the same value, guaranteeing one resolve". `mainModule` is just `{ inherit (config.__resolveResult) imports; }` — i.e. the `modules` list fed to nixosSystem is the resolved aspect imports.

3. **What the pre-pass actually does.** The fx pipeline (`nix/lib/aspects/fx/`) walks your aspects per entity/scope, dispatches policy effects, and wraps each class-module function with its context args (`class-module.nix` `wrapClassModule`), deduplicating by `class@identity` module location (`wrap-classes.nix`). That is pure Nix evaluation of your aspect data (attrsets and function application) — no nixpkgs modules are evaluated there. The expensive part (thousands of NixOS options) happens inside `nixosSystem` and is the same work you'd do by hand.

4. **The maintainers actively tune this cost.** Commit `18e0d1c` "perf: break closure chains and lazy instantiation backport (#579)" (May 2026) rewrites the fx handlers that rebuilt closure chains on every state update (which made the walk super-linear), and the resolve-result memoization in `_types.nix` exists to prevent a second resolve run.

Caveats — what I could not check:

- **No numbers.** This environment had no working `eval`, so I have no measured comparison. If it matters to you, time it yourself: `time nix eval .#nixosConfigurations.<host>.config.system.build.toplevel.drvPath` on a den template vs an equivalent hand-wired flake. Expect den to add at most a few seconds on a small fleet — the pipeline work scales with entities × aspects, while nixosSystem's module evaluation dominates.
- **One structural difference:** aspect functions are applied per entity/scope (that's what makes them parametric), so a very expensive aspect *body* is re-evaluated per entity. In hand-wired setups a module body is re-evaluated per nixosSystem call anyway, so den's extra delta is only the per-user/per-scope fan-out within a host, not per host.
- den also pulls in two extra eval-time libraries (`nix-effects`, `gen-schema` — `nix/lib/fx.nix`, `nix/lib/schema.nix`); evaluating (and on first use, fetching) them is part of the pre-pass cost. I verified the host side only; the home-manager instantiation path I did not read.

**Bottom line:** your `nixosSystem` evaluation is the same call and the same cost as hand-wiring; den adds a small, bounded, actively-optimized pre-pass. For realistic fleet sizes it is unlikely to be the dominant cost of eval.","confidence":0.7,"gaps":["No wall-clock benchmark: eval tool was unavailable in this run, so the den-vs-hand-wired timing comparison is reasoned, not measured","Did not read all of nix/lib/aspects/fx/pipeline.nix and resolve.nix — per-scope walk cost only partially mapped","Verified instantiate default for hosts (nixosSystem) only; did not verify the home-manager home.instantiate path"],"escalate_forced":"no"}

questions.question: Is a den policy essentially a transition function in a pipeline over my hosts and users?

{"answer":"Yes — that's a correct mental model, with three refinements.

**1. It is a transition function, exactly.** In den, a policy is a plain function over an entity record that returns a list of resolutions (transitions to other entities). From `denful/den` source, `modules/policies/core.nix` (main branch):

```nix
den.policies.host-to-users =
  { host, ... }:
  lib.concatMap (user: [ (resolve.shared { inherit user; }) ] ++ ...)
    (lib.attrValues host.users);
```

A function of `host` → a list of resolved `user` entities (fan-out). The docs phrase it the same way: "Policies drive topology (`host->[users]->[homes]`)" and "Den is, fundamentally, a data transformation pipeline (of your infra entities) to which functions (producing configurations) are applied" (den.denful.dev, *Core Principles*).

**2. Not just hosts and users — all entity kinds.** The same mechanism covers hosts, users, homes, and any custom kind: the same file's docs show `host-to-wsl-host` (same data shape, different entity kind) and microVM-guest branches. So it's a transition function over den's whole entity graph, of which hosts and users are the common case.

**3. Policies route data, not just topology.** The transition decides what context the downstream entity carries: `policy.resolve.shared { inherit user; }` shares the parent's context into the user scope, while `policy.resolve.to "kind" { ... }` constructs fresh entity data (the docs' `foo-to-bar` example). The docs call policies (with schema includes) "Aspect Pointcuts — where configuration is applied to data at a given point in the pipeline."

**One terminology caveat:** the policy is not the pipeline itself. The policy *defines the edges* (topology + data routing) of the entity graph; den's *resolution pipeline* is the walker that starts from `{host}`, follows those transitions, and activates aspects (via `den.schema.*.includes`) at each entity kind. So: policy = the transition function per edge, pipeline = the traversal over the graph of hosts/users/homes.

{"answer":"**Short answer: start now. There is no shipped release to wait for — the gen-based rewrite is explicitly "planned, not shipped", and it doesn't invalidate what you'd write today.**

questions.question: How are the ordinary nixpkgs NixOS modules used by den and by gen? Are they wrapped or rewritten?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**Short answer: neither, for the NixOS modules themselves.** Ordinary nixpkgs NixOS module files pass through *as-is* into nixpkgs' own `nixosSystem` in both den and gen. The "rewrite" is in a different layer: gen replaces `lib.evalModules` with a pure re-implementation for its own *definition* modules, and den is built on top of that.

**den** (`denful/den`, main @ `436350e`)
- Den's own machinery is ordinary nixpkgs-module-style code: `nix/flakeModule.nix` just imports all of `modules/` into your flake (flake-parts or plain), and the noflake template evaluates your modules with `inputs.nixpkgs.lib.evalModules` directly (`templates/noflake/default.nix`).
- An aspect's `nixos` key collects plain NixOS modules into the host's class bucket. The host is then built by the entity's `instantiate` option, whose default is **`inputs.nixpkgs.lib.nixosSystem`** (darwin → `darwinSystem`) — `nix/lib/entities/host.nix` ("Function used to instantiate the OS configuration… `nixos`: inputs.nixpkgs.lib.nixosSystem"). The docs state it plainly: "The host scope feeds its OS classes into `nixosSystem`/`darwinSystem`" (`docs/.../where-config-lands.mdx`).
- Third-party ordinary NixOS modules are used verbatim via `imports` inside an aspect's nixos module, e.g. `den.aspects.disko.nixos = { imports = [ inputs.disko.nixosModules.disko ]; }` (`docs/.../class-modules.mdx`).
- The *only* wrapping is the flat-form convenience: a den-authored class module that requests context args (`{ nixos = { host, config, ... }: ... }`) gets a partial-application wrapper (`nix/lib/aspects/fx/class-module.nix`) that pre-applies `host`/`user` and re-advertises the remaining module-system args via `lib.setFunctionArgs` — "the module never knows it was wrapped." A module that asks for no context arg passes through unwrapped (`wrapped = false`), and third-party module files are never wrapped.

**gen** (`sini/gen` hub, main @ `2963d1e`)
- Gen's *own* module system is the rewrite: `gen-merge`'s `evalModuleTree` "reproduces lib.evalModules + lib.types merge output with zero nixpkgs," and the hub's CI parity oracle holds it byte-identical to the nixpkgs engine on every axis but identity (hub README). Your `gen.tree`/`gen.modules` are "fed to gen-merge, not nixpkgs" — `gen.modules` is deliberately typed `raw`, not `deferredModule`, because nixpkgs' coercion "is a category error at the gen boundary" (`flakeModules/default.nix`).
- Your *ordinary* NixOS modules are untouched: `gen.extraModules.<node> = [ ./hardware.nix ]` is typed `attrsOf (listOf types.deferredModule)` — "these are nixpkgs NixOS modules handed to `nixpkgs.lib.nixosSystem`" — and the default `nixos` terminal is `genBind.crossing.mkHostedTerminal { evaluator = nixpkgs.lib.nixosSystem; … }`. Full nixpkgs enters *at the terminals alone*; no roster library consumes it (README: "The terminal plane is nixpkgs… the nixpkgs contact lives in the terminals a realization is handed").
- The resolved gen values cross into the nixpkgs world as *data*, not types: injected as a plain module arg (`_module.args = { genValues = … }`), so your modules read `{ genValues, ... }` while the values never enter the options tree — nixpkgs never type-walks them ("value-injection rather than type-driving", README).

So: your hardware.nix and third-party nixosModules are used exactly as nixpkgs uses them, in both. What gen rewrites is the *definition-module engine* (a pure clone of `lib.evalModules`), and den's only wrap is the optional context-arg pre-application on den-authored class modules.

questions.question: If I give a NixOS option the wrong shape inside a den aspect, does den catch it when it resolves the aspect?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**No.** Den does not type-check NixOS option values when it resolves an aspect. The shape check is delegated to the NixOS module system, and it fires later — at `instantiate`/flake-output time, not at resolve time.

**What den checks when it resolves an aspect** (denful/den @ main, read from source):

- The resolution pipeline is structural: `emit-classes` hands each class module to `class-collector`, which only assigns identity/location and dedups (`nix/lib/aspects/fx/handlers/class-collector.nix` — the state even deliberately stays lazy so the module bodies are never forced), then `wrap-classes`/`wrapClassModule` (`nix/lib/aspects/fx/wrap-classes.nix`, `class-module.nix`) binds context args and dedups. Nothing inspects the module's config values.
- The only value-level checks at that tier are about **args, not option values**: a module requesting a context arg that isn't available warns `den: class module requests '<arg>' but no <arg> context is available` and is dropped (`class-module.nix`, `wrapFunctionModule`); a den context arg colliding with a module-system arg throws by default (`den.config.classModuleCollisionPolicy` defaults to `"error"`; `emit-classes.nix` + `mkCollisionValidator` in `class-module.nix`).
- Class content is explicitly freeform: the aspect content type is `check = _: true` (`nix/lib/aspects/types.nix`, `aspectContentType`), so `nixos = { pkgs, ... }: { … }` is accepted as-is, whatever shapes sit inside. (If you enable a *strict* aspect schema, den rejects **undeclared aspect keys** on the aspect itself — that is a check on the aspect's own shape, still not on NixOS option values.)

**Where your wrong shape actually gets caught:** a resolved aspect yields `{ imports = [ …wrapped module fns… ]; }` (`nix/lib/aspects/fx/resolve.nix`; the entity's `mainModule` is exactly that list per `mainModuleOption` in `nix/lib/entities/_types.nix`). questions.question: Where do gen-types and gen-schema fill gaps in plain Nix typing? What does each one check?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Short version: **gen-types is the checking half** of the gen module system (is this value of this type? are these two types the same type?), and **gen-schema is the registry half** built on top of it (are these instances valid members of this kind? do their cross-references resolve? do they satisfy the cross-field contracts?). They sit on opposite sides of gen-merge, the byte-mode replacement for `lib.evalModules` + `lib.types`, which consumes gen-types checkers as leaf option types.

## The gaps in plain Nix typing

"Plain Nix typing" is `nixpkgs.lib.types` checked only inside `lib.evalModules`. Both READMEs position themselves against exactly that, and the gaps they each close:

1. **Closed type algebra.** `lib.types` is a fixed set of constructors; your only extension is `addCheck`, which wraps and muddies identity (gen-types' README lists measured collisions where an `addCheck`'d `int` compared equal to the stock `int`, and stock `nonEmptyListOf str` — whose `.name` is `listOf` — compared equal to `listOf str`).
2. **Open records.** Plain Nix attrsets and non-strict modules silently accept undeclared keys — typos pass.
3. **No type identity.** Nix `==` on types compares closures (functions); the verdict even diverges across evaluators (upstream Nix/Determinate compare function value slots, Lix compares objects), so there is no reliable "do these two option declarations carry the same type?"
4. **No reference types.** A string that must name an existing entity is just a string.
5. **Submodules are closed per declaration** — you can't extend `lib.types.submodule` from a downstream module.

{"answer":"**Yes — on read, `den.aspects.igloo.<name>` and `den.aspects.igloo.provides.<name>` resolve to the same sub-aspect.**

The den reference doc says it explicitly (`docs/src/content/docs/reference/aspects.mdx`, aspect-structure table, `provides`/`_` row): "`<aspect>.provides.<name>` is also reachable as `<aspect>.<name>`" — and it labels `provides` the *legacy* sub-aspect namespace, with `_` as its alias.

The source implements the aliasing in `nix/lib/aspects/types.nix` (main):

- `mergeWithAspectMeta` — the merge every declared aspect (including `den.aspects.igloo`) goes through — forwards the provides children onto the aspect's own top level: comment reads "Forward provides children onto the merged aspect so `aspect.docker` resolves to `aspect.provides.docker`", and the result is `providesChildren // merged // { … provides = …; _ = …; }`. That is why `igloo.<name>` lands on the same value as `igloo.provides.<name>`.

2. **Direct key wins on conflict** — if one name is defined in both places, the direct key shadows the provides child (`isShadowed` in `mergeWithAssetMeta`/`mkUnderscore`).
3. **Some keys must be written under `provides`:** the cross-entity keys `to-users`, `to-hosts` and `<host>` on a user aspect (per the reference doc).
4. **It's marked legacy** — the docs and code comments ("After provides removal…") indicate the direct `igloo.<name>` spelling is the current one to write.

questions.question: How deep can den aspects nest, and does including `den.aspects.foo._` include grandchildren and foo's own class keys too?

- **It does include foo's direct nested child aspects** — `foo.bar`, `foo.baz`, … (the "grandchildren" of the root `den.aspects` namespace), plus any explicit `provides` children. The bundle is built in `mkUnderscore` in `types.nix`: the synthetic aspect `foo._` has `includes = map (k: own.${k}) childKeys`, where `isChildKey k = !(isStructuralKey k) && !(classReg ? ${k}) && !(pipeReg ? ${k})`.
- **It does NOT include foo's own class keys.** Registered classes (`nixos`, `darwin`, `homeManager`, `hjem`, and custom ones like `os`) are explicitly filtered out of `childKeys` — that's what `!(classReg ? ${k})` does. - `foo`'s own class content → include `foo` itself: `[ den.aspects.foo ]`
- `foo`'s direct children → `[ den.aspects.foo._ ]`

questions.question: After updating den, putting an aspect reference in `den.schema.host.excludes` either causes infinite recursion or is ignored. What happened and what is the workaround?

questions.question: On a standalone `user@host` home, den's `inputs'` battery errors that the module argument `inputs'` is defined twice. Why?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Because a standalone `user@host` home is materialized in den as **two** entities — the `home` **and** a synthetic `user` — and the `inputs'` battery injects the `inputs'` module argument once per identity, so two modules end up defining `_module.args.inputs'` in the same module list. Den's collision check (default `collisionPolicy = "error"`) then reports the argument as defined twice.

**The mechanics, from den's source:**

1. `nix/lib/entities/home.nix`: a home declared as `den.homes.<system>."tux@igloo"` binds two module args for its aspect resolution — `config._module.args.host` (a synthetic, classless `{ name, system }` host when `igloo` isn't in `den.hosts`) and `config._module.args.user`, a **synthetic user record** `{ name = "tux"; userName = "tux"; classes = [ "homeManager" ] }` (the comment there: "A standalone home always names its user… Binding it from the home is what lets a `{ user, ... }` class module resolve at all").

2. `modules/aspects/batteries/flake-parts/inputs.nix`: the `inputs'` battery is one aspect with three sub-aspects. On your standalone home, two of them fire:
   - `hmAspect` — the home has `class = "homeManager"`, so it emits `{ key = "den.batteries.inputs'/x86_64-linux"; _module.args.inputs' = inputs' }` into `homeManager.imports`.
   - `userAspect` — unguarded, and your synthetic user has `homeManager` in its classes, so it emits a *second*, separately-constructed module of exactly the same shape into `homeManager.imports`.
   - (`osAspect` stays inert: it's gated on `host ? class`, and a standalone home's synthetic host is classless — the source guards it explicitly "the same way hmAspect already guards `home ? class`".)

   The source comment states the intent: "Imported under a key, so the module system keeps one copy when more than one of the parts below matches (**a `user@host` home is both a home and a user**)." That key-based dedup is what's failing to save you: it only merges modules the pipeline has as *shared* values; the two injections here come out of two separate scope resolutions (home-scope and user-scope), producing two distinct module values, both of which define the argument — hence the "defined twice" error from den's collision validator.

**This is a known, tracked failure in current den**, not a mistake in your config: the regression suite has `templates/ci/modules/deadbugs/standalone-qualified-home-inputs.nix`, whose first test is annotated `# FAILS: user@host standalone home, host not declared` — your exact shape (battery included on the `user@host` home, host not in `den.hosts`). Its variants show the boundaries:

questions.question: With flake-file writing npins pins for a flakeless den setup, my `follows` declarations are lost and the top-level nixpkgs-lib input is missing. Why, and what fixes it?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Both symptoms are the same root problem: **a pin file cannot express `follows`, and until very recently flake-file's npins writer had nowhere to record them.**

## Why the `follows` declarations are lost

`npins/sources.json` is a flat name→source map — there is no `follows` syntax in it. flake-file's pin writer knows this and deliberately does not pin followed inputs. In `modules/pins/default.nix` (current main):

```nix
# Collect names of inputs that set `follows` (to another input, or "" to drop it) at any
# nesting level: such an input is never fetched under its own name, so it needs no pin.
collectFollowing = ...
skipSet = lib.concatStringsSep "\n"
  (lib.subtractLists (lib.attrNames pinnableInputs) (collectFollowing inputs));
```

and `queue.bash` pre-marks those names as seen so `npins add` is never run for them. That is correct *for the pin file* — but it means the `follows` relations must be preserved somewhere else:

- **flake-file ≤ v0.7.0 (all released versions):** nothing records them. In v0.7.0 I read `modules/pins/default.nix` + `queue.bash` — the writer only emits `sources.json` and a URL sidecar; your `follows` declarations are simply dropped, and the followed inputs vanish from `sources.json` with no trace. (Even older, v0.5.0, only recognised `follows = ""` as a skip — a non-empty `follows` with a URL got a redundant pin and the relation was still lost.)
- **flake-file `main` (post-v0.7.0):** the writer now emits a sidecar, `npins/follows.nix`, containing exactly the follows you declared at every nesting level (`followsOf`/`followsNix` in `modules/pins/default.nix`, installed by `queue.bash`). **But it is inert until you feed it to `with-inputs`** — the writer does not wire it up for you.

## Why the top-level `nixpkgs-lib` is missing

In den's flake template (`den/templates/default/flake.nix`) it is declared *only* as a follows, with no URL:

```nix
nixpkgs-lib.follows = "nixpkgs";
```

The npins writer only pins inputs that have a URL (`pinnableInputs = filterAttrs (_: i: inputUrl i != null) inputs`), so a follows-only `nixpkgs-lib` gets **no pin entry at all** — it is supposed to materialise as an alias via the follows sidecar into `with-inputs`. Two things compound this for you:

1. If you aren't passing a follows spec to `with-inputs`, `nixpkgs-lib` doesn't exist in the resolved inputs — and per with-inputs' README, an unresolvable follows target "becomes `null`".
2. Since **flake-file v0.6.0** (PR #101, fixing issue #100 "Extraneous `nixpkgs-lib` input generated"), the `dendritic` module no longer auto-injects a top-level `nixpkgs-lib` — pre-#101, `modules/dendritic/nixpkgs.nix` shipped `nixpkgs-lib.follows = lib.mkDefault "nixpkgs"` for free, and after the fix it only ships the `nixpkgs` URL. So if your setup previously got it from the generated flake, upgrading made it disappear.

## What fixes it

1. **Upgrade your flake-file pin past v0.7.0** (the `main` line, where `modules/pins` writes the sidecar), then re-run `write-npins`. You'll get `npins/sources.json` **plus** `npins/follows.nix`.
2. **Pass the sidecar to `with-inputs`** in your `default.nix` (its second argument is the follows/override spec; a list combines several):

   ```nix
   with-inputs = import sources.with-inputs sources (import ./npins/follows.nix);
   # if you also need the template's local override:
   # with-inputs = import sources.with-inputs sources
   #   [ (import ./npins/follows.nix) { den.outPath = ./..; } ];
   ```

   That restores all your `follows` — including `nixpkgs-lib` as an alias of your nixpkgs channel input, which is exactly what the flake template means by it.
3. **If you actually want a real standalone `nixpkgs-lib`** (the `NixOS/nixpkgs-lib` repo, not an alias of nixpkgs), give it a URL in `flake-file.inputs` and drop the `follows` (a `follows` suppresses the pin):

   ```nix
   flake-file.inputs.nixpkgs-lib.url = "github:NixOS/nixpkgs-lib";
   ```

   It then gets its own entry in `sources.json`.

## How I know

Read from source: `denful/flake-file` `modules/pins/default.nix` + `queue.bash` and `modules/npins/npins.bash` at `main`, v0.7.0 and v0.5.0 (sidecar exists only on main; v0.7.0/v0.5.0 skip follows with no record); `modules/dendritic/nixpkgs.nix` before (#101 ref `84bff46`) and after the fix; `denful/den` `templates/default/flake.nix` (`nixpkgs-lib.follows = "nixpkgs"`, no URL) and `templates/noflake/default.nix` (with-inputs called without a follows spec); `denful/with-inputs` README (API `with-inputs sources follows outputs`, null for unresolvable follows targets).

questions.question: In den, when should a custom class be forwarded into an existing class and when should it be evaluated on its own?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"In den, the deciding factor is **who owns the final config**:

**Forward the class when its content belongs inside an existing module system's tree.** A forwarded class is sugar for a path in another class: it doesn't own a top-level config, it moves its collected modules into a target class at an attrpath. That's how den implements `user` (→ `users.users.<name>` on the host's OS class), `homeManager` (→ `home-manager.users.<name>`), `hjem`/`maid` (→ `users.users.<name>.maid`), `wsl` (→ the OS class at `wsl`), and community patterns like an `hm` alias (→ `homeManager`), a `git` class (→ `homeManager.programs.git`, guarded on `config.programs.git.enable`), or the multi-target `os`/`nix` classes (→ `nixos` *and* `darwin` / `homeManager`). The mechanism is `den.batteries.forward { each, fromClass, intoClass, intoPath, fromAspect }` (plus `guard`, `adaptArgs`, `adapterModule` for conditional forwards and arg transforms), or in new code `den.lib.policy.route`/`policy.deliver`, or declaring the destination once on the class: `den.classes.<name>.forwardTo = { class = ...; path = ...; }`. If the target may not have the options, guard the forward (e.g. `guard = { options, ... }: options ? wsl`).

**Evaluate the class on its own when it owns a top-level config** — there is no existing class to host it, and it must be instantiated with its own builder to produce its own output. Root classes (like `nixos`/`darwin`) are the ones with `den.classes.<name>.parentPath = null`, i.e. "root classes that own a top-level config". You wire them up with a custom `instantiate`/`intoAttr` (overridable per host/home) and/or `policy.instantiate`, which collects the class's modules from each scope's subtree and builds them: the terranix demo collects a per-host `terranix` class via `policy.instantiate { class = "terranix"; instantiate = { modules, ... }: modules; intoAttr = [ "terranixModules" host.name ]; }`, and a flake-module turns those raw modules into `packages`/`devShells` outputs. The `nvf-standalone` template is the same shape: a standalone neovim class that produces a `.#my-neovim` app with no NixOS/Darwin in the picture at all.

**Rule of thumb:** if you can point at an attribute path in an existing class where the content should land, forward — the class is just an alias/nesting boundary for that path (and `forwardTo` lets you declare that destination once). If the content *is* the destination — its own derivation, app, VM, or module file produced by its own builder — evaluate it on its own (`parentPath = null`, custom `instantiate`, `policy.instantiate`). A class can even forward into another custom class, as long as the chain ends at an evaluated root class.

questions.question: I wrote `options = lib.mkMerge [ (myOptions lib) ];` in a module. It half works, but forcing the whole option tree fails with an option declaration named `contents` that has type list. Why?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"The `contents` in your error is not your option — it's the internal field of the `lib.mkMerge` property.

**What `lib.mkMerge` is.** In the nixpkgs den pins (rev `64c08a7ca051951c8eae34e3e3cb1e202fe36786`, per `templates/ci/flake.lock`), `lib/modules.nix` defines:

```nix
mkMerge = contents: {
  _type = "merge";
  inherit contents;
};
```

That is a *definition property*, not an attrset merge: `{ _type = "merge"; contents = [...] }` where `contents` is always a list (the things you pass to it). It is expanded by `pushDownProperties`/`dischargeProperties` when merging **values in `config`** (e.g. `config.foo = lib.mkMerge [ a b ];`). The old flat `lib.attrsets.mkMerge` is gone — I read the full `lib/attrsets.nix` at that rev and there is no `mkMerge` there; the flat mergers are `//` and `lib.mergeAttrsList`.

**What your line does.** `options = lib.mkMerge [ (myOptions lib) ];` makes your module's `options` equal to `{ _type = "merge"; contents = [ (myOptions lib) ]; }`. The module system treats every attribute under `options` as an option declaration, so it now "declares" options named `_type` (a string) and `contents` (a list).

**The error.** `mergeModules'` in `lib/modules.nix` recurses into each name under `options`; when the subtree is not an attrset it throws:

```
An option declaration for `<path>.contents' has type `list' rather than an attribute set.
Did you mean to define this outside of `options'?
```

That's your "option declaration named `contents` that has type list".

**Why it half works.** Evaluation is lazy: as long as you only touch options declared properly by other modules, the `contents`/`_type` branches are never visited. Forcing the whole option tree (the `options` attribute of the `evalModules` result, den's schema introspection, docs generation) forces `mergeModules'` to descend into `contents` and throw. Side effect: your intended options sit at `options.contents.<name>`, not `options.<name>`, so anything that "works" is coming from other modules' declarations.

**Fix.**
- If `myOptions lib` returns a flat set of `lib.mkOption` declarations: drop the `mkMerge` and compose attrsets — `options = (myOptions lib);` or `options = (myOptions lib) // (otherOptions lib);` (or `lib.mergeAttrsList [ ... ]` for many sets).

```nix
];
```

How it works (verified in `denful/den` at `main` HEAD):

- `nix/lib/aspects/types.nix` — `mkUnderscore` builds a synthetic aspect whose body is `includes = map (k: own.${k}) childKeys`, where `childKeys` is every key on the aspect that is neither structural (`includes`, `excludes`, `provides`, `meta`, …), a registered class, nor a registered quirk/pipe — i.e. exactly its named child aspects. `mergeWithAspectMeta` then attaches this to both `provides` and `_` (`_` is a total alias for `provides`), and `aspectContentType.annotateChildren` attaches the same synthetic `._` to nested aspects, so the shorthand works at any depth: `den.aspects.foo.bar._` includes all of `foo.bar`'s children.
- The docs state it plainly: `docs/src/content/docs/reference/aspects.mdx`, aspect-structure table — "`provides` / `_`: … Included as a value, `<aspect>._` includes every depth-1 child aspect."

- Nothing is lost by using it: `<aspect>.provides.<name>` is also reachable directly as `<aspect>.<name>` (children are forwarded onto the top level), so mixing `._` includes with individual child references works as expected.

questions.question: Two modules each set `flake.checks.x86_64-linux.<name>` and only one survives. Why don't the checks merge?

function.name: reply

draft.answer:
**Short answer:** In den's standard assembly, `flake.checks` is *not a declared option* — it's a **freeform** key of the `flake` submodule, and the module system merges freeform values with a *shallow* `a // b` (`mergeDefaultOption` on `types.unspecified`). A shallow merge replaces the colliding top-level key — your `x86_64-linux` — wholesale, so the later module's entire `checks.x86_64-linux` subtree (and every check in it) silently shadows the earlier module's. The merge never descends into `x86_64-linux.<name>`, which is why no per-check merging happens.

**How it works, step by step (all checked in source):**

1. den declares `options.flake` as a freeform submodule. `denful/den` `nix/flakeOutputs.nix` (main): `flakeTop` → `manySubmodule` → `lib.types.submodule { freeformType = lib.types.lazyAttrsOf lib.types.unspecified; }`. The per-output declarations (`checks` as `systemOut = lazyAttrsOf (submodule {…})`) live in a *separate* export (`flakeOutputs.all` / `flakeOutputs.checks`) — and den's own assembly in `modules/outputs.nix` only imports `flakeOutputs.flake`, not those. So in your eval, `checks` has no option of its own.
2. nixpkgs `lib/modules.nix`: definitions that match no declared option are merged via `freeformType.merge` over `setAttrByPath`'d defs (the `freeformConfig` block), then `recursiveUpdate`'d onto the declared config.
3. nixpkgs `lib/types.nix`: `lazyAttrsOf` merges **per key**, delegating each key to the element type; `types.unspecified` has no custom merge, so `lib/options.nix` `mergeDefaultOption` applies — for attrset values that's `foldl' lib.mergeAttrs` = a **shallow** `//`.
4. Result: module B's `checks // module A's checks` → the `x86_64-linux` key is in both → B's subtree wins in full. `unspecified` accepts anything, so no error is raised; the other check just disappears.

**The fix** (den's own docs, `docs/src/content/docs/reference/output.mdx` — "the Nix module system needs to know how to merge both output definitions"; worked example `templates/ci/modules/public-api/packages-merge.nix`): declare the option for that output in a top-level module:

```nix
{ inputs, ... }: {
  imports = [ inputs.den.flakeOutputs.checks ];
}
```

That types `flake.checks` as `lazyAttrsOf (submodule { freeformType = lazyAttrsOf unspecified })`, so definitions are merged **per system**: each module's `checks.x86_64-linux` is re-evaluated as one submodule with all the definitions, and *different* check names from different modules all survive. One caveat: a *duplicate* check name within the same system is still last-wins (the value is a derivation; `unspecified` can't merge deeper than the key), so keep check names unique across modules. The docs note this import is needed when you don't use flake-parts.

questions.question: Two den aspects both include a shared nginx aspect. Will its configuration be applied twice, and how do plain Nix modules avoid double inclusion?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**No — a shared *named* nginx aspect included by two aspects is applied once per scope, not twice.** Den dedups it at resolution time; plain Nix modules dedup at collection time. Details:

## How den avoids the double application

Every `includes` entry is dispatched through the resolve chain (`den/nix/lib/aspects/fx/aspect/children.nix`, `dedupAndDispatch` → `fx.send "resolve"`), and the `gate` handler is the first step of that chain. In `den/nix/lib/aspects/fx/handlers/gate.nix` it first sends `check-dedup`:

- `den/nix/lib/aspects/fx/handlers/check-dedup.nix` — `checkDedupHandler` builds `dedupKey = "<scope>/<identity.key>"` **only if the aspect has a meaningful, non-synthetic name** (`isMeaningfulName`/`isSyntheticName` in `den/nix/lib/aspects/types.nix`: anything `<…>`-bracketed or `<anon>` doesn't key), records the key in the walk's `includeSeen`, and returns `isDuplicate = true` if that key is already there.
- `den/nix/lib/aspects/fx/identity.nix` — `identity.key` is the aspect's chain-qualified provenance: `meta.aspect-chain ++ [ name ]` (plus a `{ctxId}` instance suffix for context-fanned aspects). The chain is set when the aspect is merged and, per the `aspectMeta` comment in `types.nix`, "travels with the aspect through re-inclusion" — so the *same* nginx aspect value included via two different parent aspects gets the *same* key, no matter which path reached it.
- Back in `gate.nix`: if `isDuplicate`, the gate resumes with `{ blocked = true; result = [] }` — no class content is emitted and the sub-walk is skipped. The first inclusion is what applies.

Two caveats, both in the source:

1. **Anonymous aspects aren't deduped.** Inline includes like `{ nixos = { ... }; }` get a per-inclusion name (`<parent>/<anon>:<idx>` in `children.nix`), which carries no dedup key. `types.nix` states this explicitly: such children "resolve to an anonymous per-inclusion identity, which defeats gate dedup and duplicates their content once per path."
2. **Dedup is per scope (per entity).** The key is scope-prefixed, so the same shared aspect included into a *host* and into a *user* is applied once per entity — once in each scope, not twice in one.

## How plain Nix modules avoid double inclusion

The module system dedups by module identity at collection time, keyed on the file:

- `nixpkgs/lib/modules.nix` (master): `collectModules` → `collectStructuredModules` walks `imports` recursively; each tree node carries a `key`. In `unifyModuleSyntax`, an imported file gets `_file` **and** `key` both set to the stringified path (`unifyModuleSyntax (toString m) (toString m) (import m)`); anonymous modules get positional keys `"<parentKey>:anon-<n>"`.
- `filterModules` flattens the tree with `builtins.genericClosure` (re-exported via `lib/trivial.nix`). - `den/nix/lib/aspects/fx/handlers/check-dedup.nix` — `checkDedupHandler` builds `dedupKey = "<scope>/<identity.key>"` **only if the aspect has a meaningful, non-synthetic name** (`isMeaningfulName`/`isSyntheticName` in `den/nix/lib/aspects/types.nix`: anything `<…>`-bracketed or `<anon>` doesn't key), records the key in the walk's `includeSeen`, and returns `isDuplicate = true` if that key is already there.
- `den/nix/lib/aspects/fx/identity.nix` — `identity.key` is the aspect's chain-qualified provenance: `meta.aspect-chain ++ [ name ]` (plus a `{ctxId}` instance suffix for context-fanned aspects). 1. **Anonymous aspects aren't deduped.** Inline includes like `{ nixos = { ... }; }` get a per-inclusion name (`<parent>/<anon>:<idx>` in `children.nix`), which carries no dedup key. `types.nix` states this explicitly: such children "resolve to an anonymous per-inclusion identity, which defeats gate dedup and duplicates their content once per path."

The module system dedups by module identity at collection time, keyed on the file:

- `nixpkgs/lib/modules.nix` (master): `collectModules` → `collectStructuredModules` walks `imports` recursively; each tree node carries a `key`. questions.question: I followed docs that said `den.schema.flake-packages.includes = [ ... ]`, but my package only shows up in `nix flake show` when some host includes it. Why?

```nix
den.schema.flake-system.includes = [ den.aspects.foo ];
```

**Why your package only appeared when a host included it**

1. `den.schema` is freeform: adding a key there registers a *new* schema kind, and `den.schema.flake-packages.includes = [ ... ]` is therefore accepted without any error. But a kind's `includes` list is only consumed when an entity of that kind is actually resolved (`resolveEntity` reads `den.schema.<name>.includes` — see `nix/lib/resolve-entity.nix`). Nothing in the den pipeline ever resolves a `flake-packages` entity: the flake-output tree is driven by the kinds `flake`, `flake-system`, `flake-parts` and `default` (plus `default`). Your `includes` list was never walked, so it did nothing.

2. The reason it showed up with a host present: the per-output routes (e.g. `packages-to-flake`, which routes the `packages` class to `flake.packages.<system>`) are activated on the `flake-system` scope and cascade to every scope below it — including the host scopes that `system-to-os-outputs` resolves from `flake-system`. So when some host included your aspect, its `packages` module reached `flake.packages.<system>` through that host's include chain. Remove the host and the package disappears — the schema line was never the cause.

```nix
# once per entry in den.systems, no host required

```

```nix

{ inputs, ... }:
{
  imports = [ inputs.den.flakeOutputs.packages ];
}
```

With flake-parts the routes are live as soon as den is imported; do not import `inputs.den.flakeOutputs.*` in that case.

questions.question: My formatter's dead-code linter removed an unused `user` argument from a den class module, and now the module stopped applying. Why does an unused argument matter?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Because in den the argument list of an aspect/class module is not a binding pattern — **it is the applicability condition**. Den's pipeline introspects `builtins.functionArgs` and decides *when, where, and how many times* to apply your module from the entity-kind args it names (`host`, `user`, `home`). The `user` argument was "dead" only as far as the module body is concerned; as far as the pipeline is concerned it was load-bearing.

**How the binding works** (den `@main`, docs `explanation/parametric.mdx` + `explanation/class-modules.mdx`, source `nix/lib/can-take.nix`, `nix/lib/aspects/fx/class-module.nix`, `nix/lib/aspects/fx/handlers/compile-parametric.nix`):

When a module at scope S declares an entity-kind arg, exactly one of three things happens:
1. **In-context** → the arg binds and the module emits once, at S.
2. **Schema descendant of S** (e.g. `user` at host scope — users live under hosts) → the module **fans out once per matching descendant**. This is how a static aspect at host scope delivers per-user content: the pipeline *promotes* a class module that names a descendant kind to parametric and fans it out per user ("a class module that needs a descendant kind never silently drops its content").
3. **Neither** → the module is **inert: contributes nothing, no error, no warning** (the docs call this out explicitly as the "silent-inert footgun").

So when your linter deleted the unused `user`, the module's dispatch rule changed. The most common shape of your symptom: the module was included at host scope and targeted a user-scoped class (e.g. `homeManager`), and `user` was the thing that made it fan out per user. Without it, the module is no longer promoted/fanned out — it's emitted (if at all) only at a scope where that class isn't instantiated, and the content silently drops. Conversely, a `user` arg also *restricts* a module: `{ user, config, ... }` at a scope without a user is skipped with a `lib.warn` (class-modules.mdx, "Unsatisfied args"). Either way: the name in the pattern is the condition, and changing the pattern changed the condition.

**The fix:**
- Put the `user` argument back. If your linter flags it, silence the linter for that line rather than deleting the arg.
- **Don't rename it to `_user`** to appease the linter: the pipeline matches context keys by exact name (`ctx ? k` in `wrapFunctionModule`), so `_user` is not recognized as an entity arg — it gets advertised to the module system as an ordinary arg and the module fails or is skipped. In den, `user` must stay spelled `user` to mean "apply per user".

**How it works.** `denful/den` has no release-tracking branch (the branch list is `main` plus a few short-lived feature/test branches). Instead it maintains a floating `latest` tag:

- `.github/workflows/latest-tag.yml` triggers on `push: tags: ["v*"]` and runs `EndBug/latest-tag` with `contents: write`, which moves `latest` to the newly pushed release tag on every release.

{"answer":"**No — `lib.recursiveUpdate` does not concatenate lists.** When both sides have a list at the same attribute, the second argument (the "extension") replaces the first. Only attribute sets are merged recursively; any other type (lists included) is overridden.

Current nixpkgs master, `lib/attrsets.nix`:

```nix
recursiveUpdate =
  lhs: rhs:
  recursiveUpdateUntil (
    path: lhs: rhs:
    !(isAttrs lhs && isAttrs rhs)
  ) lhs rhs;
```

`recursiveUpdateUntil` (same file) merges via `zipAttrsWith` over `[ rhs lhs ]`: attributes present on only one side are kept as-is; present on both, it recurses only when both values are attribute sets, otherwise it takes `head values` — the value from the second argument.
```nix
lib.recursiveUpdate { a = [ 1 2 ]; } { a = [ 3 ]; }   # => { a = [ 3 ]; }
```

I read the identical definition at tags `18.09`, `19.03`, `20.03`, `21.11`, `22.05` and `23.05` too, so the behavior is consistent back at least that far.

questions.question: Why does `1 / 2` evaluate to 0 in Nix?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"`1 / 2` is 0 because in Nix, `/` between two integers is **integer division**: the result stays an integer and the fractional part is truncated toward zero. Nix integers are 64-bit two's-complement values and there is no automatic promotion to floats, so `1 / 2` → `0`.

For a real fraction, make at least one operand a float:

```nix
1.0 / 2   # 0.5
7 / 2     # 3
-7 / 2    # -3
7 / 0     # evaluation error: "division by zero"
```

**How I know**

- **Manual** (Nix Reference Manual 2.25, *Operators → Arithmetic*, nix.dev/manual/nix/2.25/language/operators): "Numbers will retain their type unless mixed with other numeric types: pure integer operations will always return integers, whereas any operation involving at least one floating point number returns a floating point number." Division by zero and integer overflow are listed as evaluation errors.
- **Source**: `NixOS/nix` (master), `src/libexpr/primops.cc`, function `prim_div`: if either operand is `nFloat` it computes a float quotient; otherwise it reads both as `NixInt` and does the C++ integer division `i1 / i2` (with an overflow check to avoid SIGFPE) and stores it with `v.mkInt`. C integer division truncates toward zero, hence `1 / 2` = `0`.","confidence":0.95,"gaps":["Did not run an eval in the sandbox to demonstrate; the result is verified from the manual and the prim_div source read instead"],"escalate_forced":"no"}

questions.question: What does `toString` give for `null`, `[ 1 2 ]`, `true` and `false`?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Short answer: the answer depends on *which* `toString`, because in the gen ecosystem there is no single one.

**`builtins.toString`** — the one gen-prelude's `toString'` delegates to, and the one current nixpkgs `lib.toString` is a re-export of:

| input | result |
|---|---|
| `null` | `""` — **empty string**, not `"null"` |
| `[1 2]` | `" [ 1 2 ]"` — bracketed, space-joined, with a leading space |
| `true` | `"1"` |
| `false` | `""` — empty string |

The Nix manual's `builtins.toString` entry says exactly this: "A Boolean (false yields `""`, true yields `"1"`)" and "null, which yields the empty string." nixpkgs' `lib.boolToString` docstring confirms the same quirk: "Calling `toString` on a bool instead returns '1' and '' (sic!)."

**gen-prelude's `toString'`** (`lib/default.nix:305`) is `value: if value == null then "null" else builtins.toString value` — the null guard exists *precisely* because `builtins.toString null` is `""`. So through `toString'` the only difference is:

- `null` → `"null"`
- `[1 2]` → `" [ 1 2 ]"`
- `true` → `"1"`
- `false` → `""`

Note: the prelude has no `toString` export at all — only `toString'`. Its `isStringLike` (in `prelude.nix`) treats `null` as string-like, which is why the guard matters there.

**Historical note:** old nixpkgs (`lib.toString` defined in `lib/strings.nix` up to 23.11) gave `"true"`/`"false"` for booleans and `"null"` for null; I read the 24.05/24.11 `lib` sources and the custom definition is no longer there in 24.05+, so behavior of `lib.toString` can differ by nixpkgs version. questions.question: Why does `"x${opt}"` fail when `opt` is null, while `toString null` works?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"It's an asymmetry in how Nix does string coercion, not a den/gen quirk — both sides live in the Nix evaluator.

**Why `"x${opt}"` fails when `opt` is null**

String interpolation (`"${...}"`) is compiled to `ExprConcatStrings`, which coerces each embedded value with `EvalState::coerceToString(..., coerceMore = false, ...)` — see `src/libexpr/eval.cc` in `NixOS/nix` (master), `ExprConcatStrings::eval`:

```cpp
auto part = state.coerceToString(
    i_pos, vTmp, context, "while evaluating a path segment", false, ...);
```

In `coerceToString` (same file), `null` is only handled inside the `if (coerceMore)` branch:

```cpp
if (coerceMore) {
    ...
    if (v.type() == nNull)
        return "";
    ...
}

error<TypeError>("cannot coerce %1% to a string: %2%", showType(v), ...)
```

With `coerceMore = false`, interpolation only accepts strings, paths, and attrsets carrying `__toString`/`outPath`. `null` (and also `int`, `float`, `bool`, lists) falls through to the final `TypeError`: **`cannot coerce null to a string`**.

**Why `toString null` works**

`builtins.toString` is `prim_toString` in `src/libexpr/primops.cc`, and it calls the *same* `coerceToString` but with `coerceMore = true`:

```cpp
auto s = state.coerceToString(
    noPos, *args[0], context, "...builtins.toString", true, false);
```

So it reaches the `nNull → ""` branch. One catch to note: `toString null` returns the **empty string `""`**, not the string `"null"` — that's documented right in the `toString` docs in that file: "`null`, which yields the empty string." So `toString` "works" by silently swallowing null.

**Fixes**

- `"x${toString opt}"` — the simplest: interpolation of a `toString` result is a string, and null becomes `""` (renders `"x"`).
- `"x${opt or ""}"` — the `or` operator yields its right side when the left is `null` (or `false`).
- If you actually want the literal text `null`: `"x${if opt == null then "null" else toString opt}"`.

**How I know:** read `NixOS/nix` master, `src/libexpr/eval.cc` (`ExprConcatStrings::eval` and `coerceToString`) and `src/libexpr/primops.cc` (`prim_toString`). I didn't run it live: the eval tool evaluates repo attributes, not arbitrary expressions, so the exact error text is from the source, not from a run on your Nix version.","confidence":0.85,"gaps":["Did not run a live `nix-instantiate --eval --expr '"x${null}"'` to confirm the exact error text on the asker's Nix version (source-derived)","Assumed `toString` means `builtins.toString`; did not check whether the asker's `opt`/`toString` comes from a specific den/gen module wrapper"],"escalate_forced":"no"}

questions.question: My function `{ a ? 1 }: a` errors when called with `{ b = 2; }`. Why, and how do I let it accept extra attributes?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**Why it fails:** `{ a ? 1 }` is a *pattern*, not an attribute access. The `? 1` only gives `a` a default; it does not loosen the pattern. A pattern without `...` is **strict**: every attribute in the argument set must be named in the pattern. `{ b = 2; }` contains `b`, which is not a formal of the pattern, so the call is rejected before your body runs.

You can see this in the Nix source (`NixOS/nix`, `src/libexpr/eval.cc`, `EvalState::callFunction` on master):

```cpp
/* Check that each actual argument is listed as a formal
   argument (unless the attribute match specifies a `...'). */
```

questions.question: What are the numeric priorities of `lib.mkForce`, `lib.mkDefault` and `lib.mkOptionDefault`, and which wins?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**Short answer:** `mkForce` = **50**, `mkDefault` = **1000**, `mkOptionDefault` = **1500** — and **`mkForce` always wins**, because the module system keeps the definition with the *numerically lowest* priority number.

## The numbers (nixpkgs `lib/modules.nix`)

In current `nixpkgs` (verified on `master`, `25.05`, `24.11`, and `23.05` — all four branches are identical for this), the three helpers are partial applications of `mkOverride` defined in `lib/modules.nix`:

```nix
mkOptionDefault = mkOverride 1500; # priority of option defaults
mkDefault       = mkOverride 1000; # used in config sections of non-user modules to set a default
defaultOverridePriority = 100;     # plain, unmarked definitions
mkForce         = mkOverride 50;
```

So the full ladder of override priorities, from strongest to weakest, is:

| helper / kind of definition | priority number |
|---|---|
| `mkVMOverride` | 10 |
| **`mkForce`** | **50** |
| `mkImageMediaOverride` | 60 |
| plain definition (no wrapper) | 100 (`defaultOverridePriority`) |
| **`mkDefault`** | **1000** |
| **`mkOptionDefault`** (the value an `mkOption`'s `default =` gets) | **1500** |

## Why `mkForce` wins

`lib/modules.nix` → `filterOverrides'` is what resolves the conflict:

```nix
filterOverrides' = defs:
  let
    getPrio = def: if def.value._type or "" == "override"
      then def.value.priority else defaultOverridePriority;
    highestPrio = foldl' (prio: def: min (getPrio def) prio) 9999 defs;
    ...
  in {
      values = concatMap (def: if getPrio def == highestPrio then [ (strip def) ] else []) defs;
```

`highestPrio` is computed with `min` over all definitions of an option, and only definitions whose priority equals that minimum survive — "highest priority" in the module system's vocabulary means the **smallest number**. So for any option you define:

- an `mkOption { default = ... }` value (1500) loses to any `mkDefault` (1000),
- which loses to any plain definition (100),
- which loses to `mkForce` (50).

`mkForce` beats everything except `mkVMOverride` (10, an internal `nixos-rebuild build-vm` thing).

If you read older docs, blog posts, or pre-22.05 code, you'll see *different* numbers: `mkForce` had `__priority = 1000`, `mkDefault` had `-100`, `mkOptionDefault` had `2`, and the **largest** value won. The module system was refactored to the `mkOverride` mechanism in 2021 (in time for 22.05), which inverted the polarity: now the **lowest** number wins, which is what you see in all releases since. The winner never changed — `mkForce` — but the direction of the numbers did, which is the source of most confusion on this topic.

questions.question: What does `let a = 1; in with { a = 2; }; a` evaluate to, and why?

function.name: reply

{"answer":"It evaluates to **`1`** — the `let` binding, not the `with` binding.

**Why:** In Nix's scoping model, `let` and `with` are two different kinds of definition, and `with` has the lower priority:

- `doc/manual/source/language/scope.md` (NixOS/nix, master): *Explicit definitions* are created by `let`, `rec` sets, and function bindings; *implicit definitions* are created **only** by `with`. - `doc/manual/source/language/syntax.md`, the "With-expressions" section states it directly: *"The bindings introduced by `with` do not shadow bindings introduced by other means,"* and gives an example that is your expression with the values swapped: `let a = 3; in with { a = 1; }; ...` keeps `a = 3`.
- The implementation matches: in `src/libexpr/eval.cc`, `EvalState::lookupVar` resolves a variable directly from its static-scope displacement when it was bound by a `let` (`if (!var.fromWith) return env->values[var.displ];`). questions.question: What does `builtins.tryEval` catch? Does it catch `abort`, and does it catch a throw nested inside an attrset?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**Short answer:** `builtins.tryEval` catches only `throw` and `assert` — it does **not** catch `abort`, and it does **not** catch a `throw` nested inside an attrset (because it doesn't look inside attrsets at all).

**How it works (current Nix, verified in source):**

`prim_tryEval` in NixOS/nix master, `src/libexpr/primops.cc`:

```cpp
try {
    state.forceValue(*args[0], noPos);   // shallow force, not deep
    attrs.insert(state.s.value, args[0]);
    attrs.insert(state.symbols.create("success"), &Value::vTrue);
} catch (AssertionError & e) {          // only this one exception type
    attrs.insert(state.s.value, &Value::vFalse);
    attrs.insert(state.symbols.create("success"), &Value::vFalse);
}
```

The error class hierarchy (`src/libexpr/include/nix/expr/eval-error.hh`) explains what that catch means:

```
EvalError
├── AssertionError        ← caught by tryEval
│   └── ThrownError       ← thrown by `throw` → caught
├── Abort                 ← thrown by `abort` → NOT caught (sibling of AssertionError)
├── TypeError             ← builtins' type errors → NOT caught
├── UndefinedVarError ...
```

- `primop_throw` throws a `ThrownError` (subclass of `AssertionError`) → caught → `{ success = false; value = false; }` (`value = false` is a legacy quirk; the source comments call it "unfortunate but removing it is a breaking change").
- `primop_abort` throws an `Abort` (direct subclass of `EvalError`, *not* of `AssertionError`) → **not caught**; it propagates out of `tryEval`.
- `assert false` raises an `AssertionError` → caught, same as `throw`.
- Builtins type errors (`TypeError`) → not caught.

This is exactly the documented caveat in the Nix 2.25 builtins manual (`nixos.org/manual/nix/stable/language/builtins.html#builtins-tryEval`): *"tryEval only prevents errors created by `throw` or `assert` from being thrown. Errors `tryEval` doesn't catch are, for example, those created by `abort` and type errors generated by builtins."*

**Nested `throw` in an attrset:**

`tryEval` performs a *shallow* force (`forceValue`), which does not recurse into attribute values. So:

```nix
let e = { x = throw ""; }; in (builtins.tryEval e).success
# => true
```

`{ x = throw ""; }` evaluates fine as an attrset — `throw` sits there as a thunk. The exception only fires later, when you access `e.x`, which happens **outside** the `tryEval`. (Same example is in the 2.25 manual.)

If you need the nested `throw` to be caught, force the value deeply first:

```nix
builtins.tryEval (builtins.deepSeq e e).success
# => false
```

`prim_deepSeq` (`forceValueDeep` on the first arg, returns the second) is the documented companion for this.

**Short answer:** `builtins.tryEval` catches only `throw` and `assert` — it does **not** catch `abort`, and it does **not** catch a `throw` nested inside an attrset (because it doesn't look inside attrsets at all).

```cpp

    state.forceValue(*args[0], noPos);   // shallow force, not deep
    attrs.insert(state.s.value, args[0]);
    attrs.insert(state.symbols.create("success"), &Value::vTrue);
```

```
├── AssertionError        ← caught by tryEval
│   └── ThrownError       ← thrown by `throw` → caught
├── Abort                 ← thrown by `abort` → NOT caught (sibling of AssertionError)
├── TypeError             ← builtins' type errors → NOT caught
```

questions.question: Why is `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` false in Nix?

questions.question: I wrote `[ f 1 ]` expecting a one-element list containing `f 1`. Why do I get two elements?

The list rule only reaches down to `expr_select`:

```yacc

  : list expr_select { ... $$.push_back($2); /* !!! dangerous */ ... }
  | { }
```

```nix

```

The same trap bites any operator inside a list: `[ 1 + 2 ]` is the two-element list `[1, 2]`, and you need `[ (1 + 2) ]`.

questions.question: An attrset with `__functor` can be called like a function, but `builtins.isFunction` says false. How should I test for callability?

function.name: reply

draft.answer:
`builtins.isFunction` is true only for actual function values, and a `__functor` set is an attrset value — the functor is never converted into a function. There is no builtin for "callable"; you test it as a disjunction, which is exactly what the evaluator itself uses to accept a "function":

```nix
let
  isCallable = x:
    builtins.isFunction x
    || (builtins.isAttrs x && x ? __functor);
in
  ...
```

**Why `isFunction` is false** — `prim_isFunction` (NixOS/nix, `src/libexpr/primops.cc`, master) does:

```cpp
state.forceValue(*args[0], noPos);
v.mkBool(args[0]->type() == nFunction);
```

A `__functor` set stays `nAttrs` after forcing, so the test is false. The functor is handled only at the call site: in `EvalState::callFunction` (`src/libexpr/eval.cc`, master) the dispatch loop contains

```cpp
else if (vCur.type() == nAttrs && (functor = vCur.attrs()->get(s.functor))) {
    callFunction(*functor->value, std::to_array({&(*allocValue() = vCur), args[0]}), vCur, functor->pos);
    ...
}
```

i.e. calling the set invokes `__functor (self, arg)` — the set itself is passed as the first argument, and the value stays a set.

**Why this predicate is the right one** — Nix's own check for "accept a function", `EvalState::forceFunction` (used by `map`, `filter`, `sort`, `foldl'`, `zipAttrsWith`, …), is:

```cpp
if (v.type() != nFunction && !isFunctor(v))  // error: expected a function
// where
bool EvalState::isFunctor(const Value & fun) const {
    return fun.type() == nAttrs && fun.attrs()->get(s.functor);
}
```

Your Nix-level `builtins.isFunction x || (builtins.isAttrs x && x ? __functor)` is a direct transcription of that, so it accepts precisely the values the evaluator would let you call without a type error.

Notes:

- `x ? __functor` only checks for the attribute's *presence* and does not force it, so the test is lazy and side-effect free — matching the C++ check, which also tests presence, not the value.
- This is a one-level check. If a `__functor` partially applies and returns *another* `__functor` set (the dispatch loop in `callFunction` keeps consuming arguments through such chains), a static test cannot prove deeper callability without applying the functor with a real argument. questions.question: I import the same anonymous module attrset twice and my list option gets duplicates. How does the module system decide two modules are the same?

{"answer":"The module system identifies a module by its **`key` attribute — not by comparing module values with `==`** — and the merge pass doesn't deduplicate at all, which is why your list option gets duplicates.

**How identity works (nixpkgs `lib/modules.nix`):**

1. Every module is normalized by `unifyModuleSyntax`, which assigns `key = toString m.key or key` — i.e. the module's own `key = "…"` attribute, or a fallback key passed in.
2. The fallback key is:
   - the **path string** for file imports (`loadModule` calls `unifyModuleSyntax (toString m) (toString m) …`), so importing the same file twice yields the *same* key;
   - a **positional placeholder** for inline/anonymous modules: `collectStructuredModules` builds them with `imap1` and fallback `"${parentKey}:anon-${toString n}"`, so your two anonymous copies get keys `:anon-1` and `:anon-2` — *distinct* modules as far as the system is concerned.
3. That key is used in exactly two places: matching `disabledModules` (`isDisabled` compares `structuredModule.key` against the disabled keys) and the `_module.graph` output. The `importApply` docstring states it plainly: "This function does not add support for deduplication … although that could be achieved by wrapping the returned module and setting the `key` module attribute."
4. The merge path never dedupes: `filterModules` flattens the module tree with `builtins.genericClosure` + `catAttrs "module"` (its comment says "unique-by-key", but nothing in the implementation enforces that), and `mergeModules` merges every occurrence.

**Why your list option duplicates:** `types.listOf` merges by concatenation — `lib/types.nix` walks *every* definition of the option and appends each entry (`value = map (x: …) evals` over all defs). Two module occurrences = two definitions = each entry twice. (`attrsOf`/`lazyAttrsOf` merge via `zipAttrsWith`, so duplicated keys merge instead of duplicate — which is why you only see it on list options.)

**What to do:**

- Import the module once: bind it in a `let` (or a file) and reference the binding once. If two parents each import the same file, restructure so only one does — shared `key` will not save you, because the merge doesn't dedupe.
- If you can't restructure, dedupe at the option level: `apply = lib.unique` on that list option (note: it affects *all* definitions of that option, so it changes semantics for other legitimate list appenders).
- If you want the module identifiable (for `disabledModules`/the graph), give it an explicit `key = "…"`.

questions.question: Reading `/etc/hostname` from my flake fails. What is the error and why?

{"answer":"## The error

Reading `/etc/hostname` from a flake fails with:

```
error: access to absolute path '/etc/hostname' is forbidden in pure eval mode (use '--impure' to override)
```

That's the exact wording — I verified it in the Nix source, `src/libexpr/eval.cc`, function `EvalState::checkSourcePath`, at tags 2.15.3, 2.16.2, 2.17.2, 2.18.8, 2.19.3 and current `master` of `NixOS/nix` (all identical):

```cpp
if (!found) {
    auto modeInformation = evalSettings.pureEval
        ? "in pure eval mode (use '--impure' to override)"
        : "in restricted mode";
    throw RestrictedPathError("access to absolute path '%1%' is forbidden %2%", abspath, modeInformation);
}
```

## Why

Flake evaluation runs in **pure-eval mode** (the `pure-eval` flake setting defaults to `true` — verified in `src/libexpr/flake/flake-settings.hh`). In pure mode the evaluator keeps an *allow-set* of readable paths, built like this (same `eval.cc`, `EvalState` constructor, all the tags above):

- `allowedPaths` starts **empty**, and the NIX_PATH / search-path entries are only added `if (!evalSettings.pureEval)` — so in pure mode it's empty at construction.
- The only paths that ever become allowed are the ones the flake machinery adds via `allowPath()`: your flake's own checked-out source directory and the source paths of your **declared inputs** (each fetched flake ref).

`/etc/hostname` is in none of those sets, so `found == false` and the `RestrictedPathError` above is thrown — before the file is even opened.

The design reason: a flake must be evaluable from its declared inputs alone. `/etc/hostname` depends on *which machine* is doing the evaluating (and changes when the machine is renamed), so letting a flake read it would make the result machine-specific and non-reproducible. Pure eval makes that dependency a hard error instead of a silent difference.

1. **Quick override:** add `--impure` (`nix eval --impure ...`, `nix flake show --impure`, etc.). Your local machine works; a CI box with a different hostname gets a different value.
2. **Hermetic fix — declare it as an input** in `flake.nix`:
   ```nix
   inputs = {
     hostname = { url = "path:/etc/hostname"; };
   }
   ```

4. **Pass it explicitly** where you control the command line: `nix build --impure --argstr hostname "$(cat /etc/hostname)"`.

questions.question: My flake uses `self.rev` for a version string, and evaluation fails with uncommitted changes. Why, and what should I use instead?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**Why:** `self` is metadata nix computes about how your flake's source was fetched. For a local checkout (a path input / `git+file://` with no `ref`/`rev`), nix uses the working tree directly. In the git fetcher (`NixOS/nix`, `src/libfetchers/git.cc`, `getAccessorFromWorkdir`), the two cases are:

- **clean tree** → the input gets `rev = <HEAD commit>` (a `000…` null-rev if the repo has no commits yet);
- **dirty tree (uncommitted changes)** → the contents no longer correspond to any commit, so **`rev` is not set at all**; instead nix records `dirtyRev = "<full HEAD>-dirty"` and `dirtyShortRev = "<short HEAD>-dirty"`, and (with the defaults `allow-dirty = true`, `warn-dirty = true` from `src/libfetchers/include/nix/fetchers/fetch-settings.hh`) prints `warning: Git tree '<path>' is dirty`.

So in a dirty checkout `self.rev` is `null` (a missing attribute), and anything that treats it as a string fails — `substring`/`lib.strings.*` on `null`, an `assert self.rev != null`, a version formatter, etc. (`toString` would silently give the literal string `"null"`.) Two related hard failures: running with `--no-allow-dirty` makes the dirty tree a straight `error: Git tree '<path>' is dirty`, and a dirty input is *unlocked* (its `dirtyRev` isn't a rev), so `nix flake lock`/`nix flake check` in pure mode refuse it with "lock file contains unlocked input" (NixOS/nix#10815). This matches the maintainer statement on NixOS Discourse: "self.rev is only non-null if your working tree is clean."

**What to use instead:**

1. **A version that tracks each commit, works dirty or clean:** `self.lastModified` (unix timestamp; set from HEAD in both cases, per the same `getAccessorFromWorkdir` code).
2. **A release version:** a checked-in file, e.g. `builtins.readFile (self.source + "/version")` — human-controlled, identical in CI and locally.
3. **If you specifically want the short rev as an identifier**, make it total:
   ```nix
   version =
     if self ? rev && self.rev != null then lib.substring 0 7 self.rev
     else (self.dirtyShortRev or "dirty");
   ```
   `self.dirtyShortRev` is exactly what nix provides for dirty trees.
4. **In CI / release pipelines**, run with `--no-allow-dirty` so a dirty checkout hard-fails instead of silently producing a `null` rev.

questions.question: I put a binary cache in my flake's `nixConfig`, but Nix asks whether to trust it or ignores it. Why?

**What's happening (Nix ≥ 2.19).** A flake's `nixConfig` can set nix.conf options, but as a security measure (a flake is code you didn't write, and letting it rewrite your global config is a privilege) only these are accepted silently: `bash-prompt`, `bash-prompt-prefix`, `bash-prompt-suffix`, `flake-registry`, `commit-lock-file-summary`. - **Interactively:** Nix asks `do you want to allow configuration setting 'substituters' to be set to '…' (y/N)?`, then offers to mark that value trusted/untrusted permanently, persisted in `~/.local/share/nix/trusted-settings.json`.
- **Non-interactively** (no TTY: scripts, CI, `nix build` from a pipeline): the prompt has no answer, defaults to N, and Nix prints

questions.question: Why does nixpkgs expose `legacyPackages.<system>` rather than `packages.<system>` in its flake?

function.name: reply

> The "legacy" in `legacyPackages` doesn't imply that the packages exposed through this attribute are "legacy" packages. But when the Nix CLI sees a `legacyPackages` attribute it displays `omitted` instead of evaluating all packages, which keeps `nix flake show` on Nixpkgs reasonably fast, though less information rich.
>
> The reason why finding the tree structure of `legacyPackages` is slow, is that for each attribute in the tree, it is necessary to check whether the attribute value is a package or a package set that needs further evaluation. Evaluating the attribute value tends to require a significant amount of computation, even considering lazy evaluation.

Concretely:

- **`legacyPackages.<system>` is the full pre-flake package set** — the file defines it as `forAllSystems' (system: import ./. { inherit system; ... })`, i.e. exactly what `import <nixpkgs> { inherit system; }` used to return (all ~20k packages plus `lib`, `stdenv`, `pkgs*`, etc.). questions.question: Should I bump `system.stateVersion` when I upgrade NixOS to a new release?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**Short answer: no — you generally should *not* bump `system.stateVersion` when upgrading to a new release. Current NixOS guidance is that most users should never change it after the initial install.**

**What `system.stateVersion` means now**
It records the *first version of NixOS installed on that machine*, and it's used to keep compatibility with application data (databases, `/var/lib` paths, …) created under older releases. Modules gate changes on it with checks like `lib.versionAtLeast config.system.stateVersion "26.05"` so that a system that was installed with an older release keeps the old defaults. It does **not** control which Nixpkgs you build from — changing it does not upgrade your system at all.

**What to do to upgrade instead**
Point your input at the new release (switch your `nixos` channel, or update the `nixpkgs`/`nixos` flake input), then `nixos-rebuild switch` (or `--upgrade`). That's the whole procedure.

**What the source says**
- `nixos/modules/misc/version.nix` (nixpkgs master), the definition of `system.stateVersion`:
  - "Most users should **never** change this value after the initial install, for any reason, even if you've upgraded your system to a new NixOS release."
  - "This value does **not** affect the Nixpkgs version your packages and OS are pulled from, so changing it will **not** upgrade your system."
  - "This value being lower than the current NixOS release does **not** mean your system is out of date, out of support, or vulnerable."
  - The option has an assertion (value must be `YY.MM`) whose message says: *"If you want to switch releases or switch to unstable, you should change your channel and/or flake input URLs only. **DO NOT** touch the 'system.stateVersion' option, as it will not help you upgrade. Leave it exactly on the previous value."*
  - The default is now `config.system.nixos.release` (the release of the Nixpkgs in use), with a warning urging you to set it explicitly at install time — so having a value older than your current release is expected and fine.
- `nixos/modules/installer/tools/tools.nix`: the `nixos-generate-config` template embeds the same text in the generated `configuration.nix` (`system.stateVersion = "…"; # Did you read the comment?`).
- The manual's "Upgrading NixOS" chapter (`nixos/doc/manual/installation/upgrading.chapter.md`) describes upgrading purely as switching channels / updating flake inputs + `nixos-rebuild switch --upgrade`, and doesn't ask you to touch `stateVersion` at all.

**When bumping *is* the right move**
Only when a service you run has a state-version-gated data change and the release notes tell you to migrate. Bumping flips all those `stateVersion >=` conditionals at once, so you must read the new release's release notes first. questions.question: I changed a user's password with `passwd` and after a rebuild it was reset. Why, and which option controls this?

If your config doesn't set any password option for that user, the result is a locked password.

**Which option controls it:** `users.mutableUsers` (default `true`). From the users module source (`NixOS/nixpkgs`, `nixos/modules/config/users-groups.nix`, branch `nixos-25.05`):

- `mutableUsers = true`: existing `/etc/passwd`/`/etc/shadow` entries are *merged* on activation — "the initial password for a user will be set according to `users.users`, but existing passwords will not be changed." A `passwd`-set password survives rebuilds.
- `mutableUsers = false` (warning): "the contents of the user and group files will simply be replaced on system activation. This also holds for the user passwords; all changed passwords will be reset according to the `users.users` configuration on activation."

questions.question: In gen-types, what does a checker's `verify` return for a valid value and for an invalid one?

{"answer":"In gen-types, a checker's `verify` is the contract-checking boundary:

- **Valid value → `null`.** Success is `null`, not `true` — `null` means the value inhabits the type.
- **Invalid value → an error string** (the "blame string") describing the mismatch. `verify` does not throw; it returns the string as its result. The sibling `check` field is the throwing variant: it runs `verify` and does `if e == null then v2 else throw e`.

Example straight from the README:

```nix
t.int.verify 5   # => null
t.int.verify "x" # => "expected type 'int' but value \"x\" is of type 'string'"
```

The message is built by `typeError` (`"expected type '<name>' but value <rendered> is of type '<typeOf v>'"`, with the value rendered shallowly — containers show names/length, members are `…`), and nested composites thread context frames via `addContext`:

```nix
(t.checkedAttrsOf (t.checkedListOf t.int)).verify { a = [ 1 "x" ]; }
# => "in attrsOf<listOf<int>> value: in listOf<int> element:
#     expected type 'int' but value \"x\" is of type 'string'"
```
