questions.question: Does gen-graph's `topoOrder` throw on a cyclic graph? What do I read from the result?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**No — on a cycle `topoOrder` does not throw.** It returns a value: `{ ok = false; cycles = … }`. The throwing layer is `phaseOrder`.

## What you read from the result

The call is `topoOrder { keyOf ? id; lessThan ? builtins.lessThan } { nodes; edges; … }` (options record first, then the accessor) and it returns one of:

- **`{ ok = true; order = [ node; … ] }`** — a producers-first topological order. Edge direction is `edges u ∋ v` = "u depends on v", so every node appears *after* everything it depends on. On success there is **no `cycles` attribute at all** (`(result) ? cycles` is `false`) — that's the live control the suite pins.
- **`{ ok = false; cycles = [ [ node; … ]; … ] }`** — `cycles` is a list of **strongly-connected-component member sets**: every node that lies on any cycle, grouped by its SCC, **sorted within each component, all components in one pass**. Fix one and you don't meet the next (nixpkgs' old `toposort` reported only the first cycle found). A **self-loop is reported as its own singleton**: `{ ok = false; cycles = [ [ "a" ] ] }`.

So the normal consumer pattern is `if r.ok then r.order else …` and you can render your own diagnostic from the member sets — that non-throwing shape is deliberate: the consumers that drove it (the retired gen-pipe, gen-edge) build their own per-edge diagnostics from the member sets. If you want the legacy throw-on-cycle contract, call `phaseOrder` instead, which throws `gen-graph.phaseOrder: cyclic ordering constraints: <json of the cycles>`.

Note what *does* throw: shape refusals, all named and catchable (`tryEval`-able) — a non-string `keyOf` output, two nodes sharing one key, an edge naming a node outside `nodes`, a graph record missing `nodes`/`edges`, or a misspelt option. A cycle is not among them. (Migration hazard: if you're still calling the old one-record form `topoOrder { nodes; edges; }`, the record is now handed to the *options* set and refused by name — move the graph to the second argument.)

Cost, for completeness: the `ok = false` path pays the cycle report on top of the Kahn loop — it runs the Tarjan/lowlink partition twice (once for `cycles`, once for `sccOf`), Θ((n + m)·log₈ n). The success path pays neither.

questions.question: Why does gen-prelude ship its own `hasInfix` instead of using nixpkgs' `lib.hasInfix`?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Two reasons, and they're not alternatives: the dependency structure makes nixpkgs' `lib.hasInfix` unavailable in the first place, and the behaviour of nixpkgs' version makes it unusable even where nixpkgs is in scope.

**1. gen-prelude is the nixpkgs-lib-free base, so `lib` doesn't exist there.**
The library is the "small pure-utility dependency that lets the pure gen substrate drop `nixpkgs.lib`": its flake declares **zero inputs** and imports nothing from nixpkgs.lib, so a consumer's lock gains no transitive nixpkgs from pulling it in. Purity is enforced structurally (there is no `lib` to draw from) and asserted by a purity suite that token-scans the library source for `nixpkgs`, `lib.`, `{ lib }`, `evalModules`, `mkOption`. Calling `nixpkgs.lib.hasInfix` from inside it would be the very violation the scanner exists to red — it would re-tether the whole 18-consumer ecosystem to nixpkgs. So the function has to be the library's own (README, `sini/gen-prelude` @ `main`).

**2. nixpkgs' `lib.hasInfix` overflows the C stack on long strings; the vendored copy is linear.**
This is documented in the definition's own comment (`sini/gen-prelude` @ `main`, `lib/default.nix`):

```nix
hasInfix = infix: content: infix == "" || length (split (escapeRegex infix) content) > 1;
```

I checked what nixpkgs actually does (`NixOS/nixpkgs` @ `master`, `lib/strings.nix`):

```nix
hasInfix =
  infix:
  let
    matchGivenInfix = builtins.match ".*${escapeRegex infix}.*";
  in
  ...
  content: matchGivenInfix "${content}" != null;
```

The `.*` anchors on both sides make the regex engine (std::regex) recurse to a depth proportional to the string length, which overflows the C stack when scanning whole source files — an uncatchable abort (`tryEval` does not contain it). gen-prelude's split-based version carries no `.*` anchors and scans linearly, and answers the same boolean as nixpkgs (the repo's prelude-fidelity suite asserts byte-identity against `lib.hasInfix`/`lib.escapeRegex`, including per-metacharacter arms; the vendored `escapeRegex` uses the same twelve metacharacters and the same `replaceStrings` fold).

**Why the library even needed to ship it:** the purity suite's scanner *is* this library's own `hasInfix` scanning its own source (verified in `ci/tests/purity.nix` @ `main`): "nixpkgs `lib.hasInfix` overflows the C stack on whole-file source (its `.*needle.*` recurses to depth ∝ string length), which is why every purity suite in the ecosystem takes `genPrelude.hasInfix`". The `ci/` harness legitimately has nixpkgs in scope, so the reason it uses the vendored copy is the stack behaviour, not the purity rule — and the purity suite even carries a detector cell that would catch a `hasInfix` broken to always answer false.

questions.question: In gen-schema, what happens when an instance sets a key its kind does not declare?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"It throws at eval time — and by default that's the behavior, because kinds are strict by default.

**What you get** (a catchable `throw`, naming every offending key at once, each with a fix line):

```
STRICT MODE: "addrr", "net.mtuu" are not declared on host (instance at hosts.web, defined in /etc/nixos/hosts.nix).
Fix: schema.host.options.addrr = mkOption { ... };
Fix: schema.host.options.net.mtuu = mkOption { ... };
```

Keys that aren't bare Nix identifiers (e.g. containing a dot) are printed quoted, so the suggested fix parses as written.

**How it works** (from `sini/gen-schema` @ `main`):
- `lib/instance.nix` — `mkInstanceTypeCore` takes `strict ? kindValue.strict` (the kind's flag), and into every instance's submodule imports it puts either `mkStrictModule kind` (strict) or `{ config._module.freeformType = merge.types.attrsOf merge.types.anything; }` (freeform).
- `lib/strict.nix` — `mkStrictModule` sets the instance's `_module.freeformType` to a custom type named `strict` whose `merge` **always throws**. - **Signature:** `evalModuleTree { specialArgs ? {}; check ? true; prefix ? []; coreShortCircuit ? false; warmFrom ? null; editedModules ? []; class ? null } modules → { config; options; type; provenance; undeclared; deprecations; _type; class; extendModules; graph }`.
- **Inputs it demands:** four *required* injected libraries — `prelude` (gen-prelude), `types` (gen-types leaf checkers), `memo` (gen-memo), `scope` (gen-scope, the graph evaluator; gen-merge "drives no fixpoint of its own"). - **Role in the ecosystem:** the "merge half" of a two-part split — gen-types answers "is this value well-typed?", gen-merge answers "how do these definitions combine into one value?"; they meet only at leaves, post-merge. 1. **It is a re-implementation of the same engine, with nixpkgs as the reference.** The README's yardstick ("byte-mode"): `lib.evalModules` is the reference implementation and "the same modules must yield the same config, down to the priority-resolved winner at every option" — with zero nixpkgs in `lib/` (the library is checked nixpkgs-lib-free by `ci/tests/purity.nix`, and parity cells run the same constructions through both engines against live nixpkgs, `ci/tests/parity-surface.nix`). questions.question: How do I run a gen library's tests locally, and why is `nix flake check` at the repo root not enough?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**Run the suite from the library repo root with the `ci` devshell command, not `nix flake check` at the root:**

```
nix develop ./ci --command ci
```

Targeted runs, from the same devshell:

- `ci <suite>` — one suite (diagnostic; stops after the suite)
- `ci <suite>.<test>` — one test (routed through the `testSingletons` view, because a bare `tests.<suite>.<test>` leaf makes nix-unit report a silent `0/0 successful`)
- `ci --tests-error` — the error plane: cells whose `expr` can *abort* live on the separate `flake.testsError` output (`ci/tests-error.nix`), read by `nix-unit --flake ./ci#testsError`, judged both by the host evaluator and by `checks.tests-error`
- `ci --tests-process` — the process plane
- plus `fmt`, `repl`, and `relock` (bumps the repo's locks, root then ci)

The bare `ci` is the full local gate. In order (gen-harness `flakeModule.nix`, the `ci` command):
1. it runs the **read-roots guard** (`<name>-ci-read-roots`) *before* nix-unit — it refuses on any untracked file under the suite's declared read roots (`ci/tests/`, declared `readRoots`, `examples/`); the remedy is `git add` or move;
2. it runs `nix-unit --flake ./ci#tests` (all cells);
3. it then **builds every declared check** of the `ci` flake except `tests-error` — including `checks.default`, the batch asserter, which re-forces every `expr` and also refuses cells that belong on the wrong plane.

**Why `nix flake check` at the repo root is not enough — two separate reasons:**

1. **The tests are not in the root flake.** Each gen library's root `flake.nix` is the *library* flake. I read `sini/gen-graph/flake.nix` at `main`: it exports exactly `lib = import ./. { prelude = gen-prelude.lib; }` and declares no `checks` at all. The test suite lives in the sibling **`ci/` sub-flake**, built on `gen-harness.lib.mkCi`, which `import-tree`s the whole `ci/tests/` directory (gen-graph's `ci/flake.nix`: `testModules = ./tests`). So `nix flake check` at the root has no tests to build; you need at least `nix flake check ./ci`.

2. **Even `nix flake check ./ci` is unguarded, and that's the real trap.** A bare `nix flake check ./ci` runs the suite against a **git-filtered copy of the tree** — it is blind to untracked cells. A new test file under `ci/tests/` that you haven't `git add`ed simply never enters the suite: `import-tree` only sees committed content, so you get a green that wasn't computed over your tree. The guarded `nix develop ./ci --command ci` exists for exactly this: the read-roots guard runs first and **refuses** when an untracked file sits under a declared read root — fail-closed instead of fail-open. (The pre-commit hooks `ci` and `ci-error` run the same guarded entry on every `.nix` file, so you can't walk through the hole by habit either.)

questions.question: I ran `nix-unit --flake ./ci#tests.<suite>.<cell>` on one gen test and it printed `0/0 successful` with exit 0. Did my test pass?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"No — `0/0 successful` means **no test ran at all**. The exit 0 is vacuous, not a pass.

**Why.** In `nix-community/nix-unit` (`src/nix-unit.cc`, `main` branch):

- With `--flake`, the fragment is the entry point: `vRoot = flake.toValue(*state)`, i.e. the value of `tests.<suite>.<cell>`.
- Since you passed no `-A`, it calls `recurseTests({}, vRoot)`, which **only runs attributes whose name starts with `test`** (`name.rfind("test", 0) == 0`); any other child is only recursed into.
- A single test *case* (a `denTest` cell) is an attrset whose children are `expr` / `expected` (or `expectedError`) — none of which starts with `test`. So pointing the fragment at one case yields zero matching attributes: `results = {total = 0, success = 0}`.
- And the exit status is computed as `bool success = results.success == results.total;` → `0 == 0` → true → prints `🎉 0/0 successful` and exits 0. nix-unit never distinguishes "all tests passed" from "no tests found".

So what you hit is the classic false green: the path exists (a typo would have been an eval error, not a 0/0), but it points at a leaf test whose children don't match the `test*` prefix. The same 0/0 happens if a case is named without a `test` prefix — nix-unit is blind to non-`test*` names, even at the suite level.

questions.question: Which gen library mints identities, and what does an identity look like?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**`gen-identity`** (`sini/gen-identity`) is the only library that mints identities. Its README states it directly: "`hashIdentity` is the one minting authority for the gen ecosystem; nothing else mints" (ruling 5 of ADR-0016). It was relocated whole from `gen-schema`; `gen-schema` keeps only the reflection half — deciding which of a kind's options are identity keys and stamping `id_hash` onto instances (`mkIdentityModule`) — and builds that by calling into the mint injected. It is deliberately its own dependency-free library (builtins only, zero flake inputs) so that any library — e.g. `gen-types`, which sits below `gen-schema` — can reach it without closing a flake cycle.

**What an identity looks like** — a single string:

```
identity = "<kind>:" + sha256(<pairs preimage>)
```

from `lib/default.nix` (main): `hashIdentity` ends in

```nix
"${builtins.unsafeDiscardStringContext kind}:"
+ builtins.hashString "sha256" (canonicalPreimage kind labels valueOf);
```

with signature `hashIdentity : kind -> labels -> valueOf -> "<kind>:<sha256hex>"`. The README's own example:

```nix
hashIdentity "bobbin" [ "name" "thread" ] (k: { name = "lark"; thread = "linen"; }.${k})
# → "bobbin:9e7fccd3…"
```

Key properties of the shape, straight from the source:

- **The kind rides outside the digest.** The preimage is a digest of the ⟨label, value⟩ pairs alone; the kind tag is joined on top. That keeps the digest region kind-independent, and the kind stays recoverable by splitting on the first colon — which is why `:` is refused in a kind name.
- **The preimage is a bounded, type-tagged canonical encoding** of the pairs: each node is type-tagged (`s…` JSON-quoted strings, `b1`/`b0` bools, `i…` ints, `f…` floats with |v| < 2⁵³ with integral floats normalised to `i`, `z` null, lists as `[…]`, records as `{…}` with `attrNames`-sorted keys, so order-insensitivity is by construction). The bounds are a 65,536-character preimage budget and a 512-level walk depth.
- **What cannot be encoded is refused by name, never partially hashed**: a lambda, a path, a derivation (the full three-attribute `type = "derivation"` + `drvPath` + `outPath` shape), floats with |v| ≥ 2⁵³, empty/non-string kinds, `:` in a kind, zero labels, non-string labels, duplicate labels, and budget/depth exhaustion. A refusal reads as e.g. `identity: a lambda in an identity position; kind "attaches", label "entity"`.
- **Equality follows Nix `==` in both directions** — neither coarser nor finer — over the admitted domain, so structurally equal values mint one identity.

**How I know:** I read `sini/gen-identity`'s `lib/default.nix`, `default.nix`, `flake.nix` and `README.md` (main branch) directly, plus the hub README of `eaal/nix-gen` (the gen roster, which lists `gen-identity` as "The ecosystem's single minting authority"). questions.question: I evaluate a custom den class with lib.evalModules and want to turn the resulting config into a YAML file. How do I generate it, and do I need to strip `_module` from the config first?

function.name: reply

draft.answer:
**Short answer:** generate it with `lib.generators.toYAML { } config` (which is just `builtins.toJSON` — JSON is valid YAML), applied to the **`.config`** of your `lib.evalModules` result. You do **not** need to strip `_module` yourself: nixpkgs already strips the top-level `_module` from `.config` before it hands it to you.

## How to generate the YAML

```nix
{ pkgs, lib, ... }:
let
  res = lib.evalModules {
    modules = [
      # your custom den class modules
    ];
  };
  cfg = res.config;   # <- this one, not the whole result
in
pkgs.writeText "my-class.yaml" (lib.generators.toYAML { } cfg)
```

That file is a compact single-line JSON document, which any YAML 1.2 parser (yq, python-yaml, ruby, …) reads fine. If you want pretty multi-line YAML, reformat in a derivation:

```nix
let
  json = pkgs.writeText "cfg.json" (lib.generators.toYAML { } cfg);
in
pkgs.stdenv.mkDerivation {
  pname = "my-class.yaml";
  nativeBuildInputs = [ pkgs.yq ];
  installPhase = "yq -yP ${json} > $out";
}
```

**Source check (NixOS/nixpkgs master):**
- `lib/generators.nix`: `toYAML = { }: lib.strings.toJSON;` with the comment "YAML has been a strict superset of JSON since 1.2, so we use toJSON."
- `lib/modules.nix`, end of `evalModules`: the result is
  `{ _type = "configuration"; options = …; config = removeAttrs config [ "_module" ]; _module = config._module; graph = …; extendModules = …; type = …; class = …; }`
  — i.e. `_module` is a *sibling* of `config`, and the `config` attribute you receive is already `removeAttrs config [ "_module" ]`.

## When you *do* have to strip

- **If you serialize the whole result** (`builtins.toJSON res`), it throws: `options` contains `__toString` functions, `extendModules` is a function, `type` is an option type. Either take `.config`, or `builtins.removeAttrs res [ "_type" "options" "_module" "graph" "extendModules" "type" "class" ]` first.
- **If a module writes a `_module` key into a *nested* freeform path** (not at the top of a module evaluation), nixpkgs' stripping doesn't reach it — filter those out yourself.
- **Functions in `config`** break `toJSON` ("cannot coerce a function to JSON"). Make sure your class is fully evaluated (aspect/module lambdas called with their args) before serializing. Derivations are fine — they serialize as store-path strings.

## Den-specific note

Den itself ships no YAML helper (nothing in `nix/lib/` — checked `nix/lib/default.nix`), so the nixpkgs generator is the standard tool. If your custom class is built with `den.batteries.forward`, the battery internally sets `config._module.freeformType = lib.types.lazyAttrsOf lib.types.unspecified` on the forwarded sub-module (`nix/lib/forward.nix`), but that lives inside that sub-module's own `evalModules`, whose `.config` nixpkgs strips — including for every nested `types.submodule` value (`lib/types.nix`, `submoduleWith` merge returns `configuration.config`). So a forwarded class's merged content won't drag a stray `_module` into your output.

## Caveats

- I verified all of the above against nixpkgs **master** source and den **main** (`sini/den`); I did not evaluate your actual class (no repo/rev given), and I didn't check that `lib.generators.toYAML` exists in your specific nixpkgs release (it's present on master; `builtins.toJSON` works on all of them).

1. **Get the lib without the framework.** Add den as a flake input and put `inputs.den.nixModule inputs` in your module list. `nixModule` (see `nix/default.nix`) is `inputs: { config, lib, ... }: (den-lib { inherit inputs config lib; }).nixModule`, and `nix/nixModule/lib.nix` sets `config.den.lib = den-lib` — nothing else from the framework is pulled in (contrast `inputs.den.flakeModule`, which imports all of `modules/`).

- Collection is driven by the tree you hand the resolver. `den.lib.aspects.resolve <class> <tree>` (and `resolveImports`, which skips entity instantiation and just returns `{ imports = [ … ] }`) walks the tree and, at every visited aspect, emits every key equal to the target class — even for unregistered classes. That's in `nix/lib/aspects/fx/key-classification.nix`: `isClassKey = k: classRegistry ? k || (targetClass != null && k == targetClass)`.
- But activation is include-based: sub-aspects nested under a freeform key are "classified but never auto-walked — they activate via explicit `includes`" (`nix/lib/aspects/fx/handlers/compile-static.nix`, and the matching comment in `key-classification.nix`). The compile-static handler only walks `includes` + policies. So if you pass the raw `den.aspects` namespace attrset as the resolution root, its top-level aspects are nested keys and nothing gets collected.

Practical options:

1. One-shot collection from all aspects — build the aggregation root programmatically instead of a named aspect:
   ```nix
   den.lib.aspects.resolveImports "myClass" { includes = lib.attrValues den.aspects; }
   ```
   The walk covers every root aspect (and their includes closure); the gate dedups by identity, so an aspect reachable through several paths is emitted once per scope.
2. Persistent/global wiring — `den.default` is den's global root aspect (`test-pair-of-hosts` in `templates/ci/modules/public-api/forward-from-custom-class.nix` uses `den.default.includes = [ … ]` for exactly this kind of fleet-wide wiring). A named aggregating aspect is the same idea, just more explicit.
3. Per-entity delivery, which is the normal case: register the class (`den.classes.<name> = { … }`) and attach `den.batteries.forward` (or `den.lib.policy.route`) to the entity schema or the aspects that need it. Then every host/user resolution collects the class from its own aspect tree — that's how `user`, `homeManager`, `persys` and all the `forward-*.nix` feature tests work, and it's what you want if the content lands in `users.users.<name>` etc.

Caveat for option 1: parametric aspects (`{ host, … }: { myClass = …; }`) only resolve when their context args are present; a namespace-wide resolve without a host/user context defers them (the post-assembly drain in `nix/lib/aspects/fx/resolve.nix` only drains deferred includes whose args are available). So a single all-of-`den.aspects` resolve collects the *static* class content; context-dependent content belongs to the per-entity path (option 3).

questions.question: Does using den make Nix evaluation of my NixOS systems slower than wiring nixosSystem by hand?

- One `nixosSystem` per host, exactly like hand wiring. questions.question: Is a den policy essentially a transition function in a pipeline over my hosts and users?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Yes — that's essentially the right mental model, with two refinements the source bears out (checked against `denful/den@main`: `docs/src/content/docs/explanation/policies.mdx`, `nix/lib/aspects/fx/policy/{dispatch,iterate,default}.nix`, `modules/policies/core.nix`, `AGENTS.md`).

**What a policy is, per the source**

- A policy is "a function from context to a list of effects"; the pipeline calls it only when its argument signature is satisfied by the current scope context — e.g. `{ host, ... }:` fires only where a `host` is in context (`dispatch.nix` checks `resolveArgsSatisfied` per entry).
- The effects are a typed vocabulary: `resolve` (enrich the current scope, *or* spawn a child entity scope), `include`, `route`, `provide`, `exclude`, `instantiate`, `spawn`, `pipe` (`validEffectTypes` in `dispatch.nix`).
- The pipeline around it is a fixed-point loop over the scope context: "dispatch, enrich, re-dispatch until stable" (`iterate.nix`, `maxPolicyIterations = 10`; a non-converging cycle throws `den: enrichment cycle at <kind>`). So in the state = scope-context sense, a policy firing *is* a transition: context → (enriched context, list of pending effects).

So "transition function in a pipeline over hosts and users" is fair — two caveats:

1. **Not just hosts and users.** The built-in policy graph also has `flake` / `flake-system` / `system` nodes (`flake-to-systems`, `system-to-os-outputs`, `system-to-hm-outputs`), and the entity kinds extend to `home` plus anything you declare via `den.schema` (batteries add kinds like `wsl-host`; the microVM template makes guests entities). `host-to-users` in `modules/policies/core.nix` is the host→user edge: it fans each host out to its declared users, each becoming its own child scope. Per `AGENTS.md`, the "scope tree emerges from policy-driven context expansion."

2. **The policy doesn't mutate the state itself.** It's a pure producer of effect values; the handlers (the algebraic-effects trampoline in `nix/lib/aspects/fx`) apply them — opening child scopes, injecting aspects, routing class modules. So a policy is better read as a *transition rule* evaluated by the pipeline's interpreter, with firing gated on argument satisfaction and the loop running to a fixed point.

If your question is really "will my `den.policies.X = { host, ... }` fire where I expect": it fires in any scope where `host` is in context and the policy is active (registered in an `includes` list — globally, per entity kind via `den.schema.host.includes`, or on an aspect's subtree; `excludes` override), and its `resolve` effects with entity keys open child scopes. ## den (`github.com/denful/den`, `main`)

- Den is itself built on the nixpkgs module system: its options (`den.aspects`, `den.hosts`, `flake.*` outputs) are ordinary `lib.mkOption`/`submodule` options, and its flake pipeline is evaluated with `lib.evalModules` (`modules/outputs.nix`: `lib.evalModules { modules = [ flakeModule inputs.den.flakeOutputs.flake ]; specialArgs.inputs = inputs; }`).
- The `nixos` class is realized with the standard nixpkgs system builder: the `host.instantiate` option defaults to **`inputs.nixpkgs.lib.nixosSystem`** (`nix/lib/entities/host.nix`, same file sets `intoAttr` → `nixosConfigurations`), and the host's `mainModule` is `{ inherit (config.__resolveResult) imports; }` — the resolved aspect content becomes the `imports` list of the NixOS module set.

questions.question: Where do gen-types and gen-schema fill gaps in plain Nix typing? What does each one check?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Short version: plain Nix has no type system at all — type discipline only exists inside nixpkgs' `lib.evalModules`/`lib.types`, and that layer has three real gaps: **no value-level checking outside the module system**, **name-based type identity that lies**, and **no stable equality/identity for comparing and deduplicating values**. gen-types fills the first two (the checking half), gen-schema fills the registry/identity side (the instance half). The layering is `gen-prelude → gen-types → gen-merge → gen-schema` (`gen-schema/flake.nix` header; gen-types is a leaf *below* gen-schema so it can be imported without a flake cycle).

## gen-types — what it checks

A pure, nixpkgs-lib-free **structural type checker**: "the checking half of the pure-gen module system" (`gen-types` repo description; `lib/checkers.nix` header). A type is a predicate boundary (contract checking, Findler & Felleisen 2002): `verify: value → null | errString`. No merging, no priorities, no fixpoint — gen-merge sits above and calls these checkers to verify leaves.

It checks two things:

1. **That a value inhabits a type.** Verified in source (`lib/checkers.nix`):
   - primitives: `string`, `int`, `bool`, `float`, `number`, `path`, `pathLike`, `attrs`, `list`, `function`, `derivation`, `null`, `any`, `never` (builtins wrappers; `path`/`function` use the nixpkgs predicates as vendored in gen-prelude).
   - combinators: `checkedOption`, `checkedListOf`, `checkedAttrsOf`, `union`, `intersection`, `enum`, `tuple`, `optionalAttr`.
   - `struct name { members }`: record checking with `total` (every member present, `optionalAttr` exempt) and `unknown` (closed world — undeclared keys rejected) policies plus an optional whole-record invariant; `.override` composes deltas.
   - `refined base [{check, message}]` (`lib/refined.nix`): base verified first, then predicate contracts in one pass; stock set `positive`, `nonEmpty`, `tcpPort`.
   - `strict` (closed-world key check) and `mkValidator`/`runValidators` (named predicates over instances, collected into an Either).
   - Errors thread context through nesting — `in attrsOf<listOf<int>> value: in listOf<int> element: expected type 'int' but value "x" is of type 'string'` — with a shallow, total, 256-byte-bounded value renderer, so a refusing value can never abort the refusal, and names of self-referential types stay finite (the `__okAt` step-indexed guard).

2. **That types have an identity.** `typeEq`/`idOf` mint identity over the **construction** (constructor + argument values), never the name. The `checkers.nix` header documents four *measured* name-only collisions this fixes: `refined int positive == refined int tcpPort`, `strict ["a"] == strict ["b"]`, `enum "colour" ["red"] == enum "colour" ["blue"]`, `struct "cfg" {a=int} == struct "cfg" {a=str}` — all answered true under name minting, i.e. semantically distinct values admitted under one type (Milner 1978 §3.3). nixpkgs `lib.types.*` records are compared, never minted (they claim a constructor without declaring one — an `addCheck`'d int installed via `lib.extend` compared equal to stock int).

Gaps it fills in plain Nix typing: value-level checking without dragging in nixpkgs' lib; correct type identity where name-based identity was false; total, bounded, context-threading error rendering where plain Nix gives uncatchable aborts or generic messages.

## gen-schema — what it checks

A **typed record registry** "with extension points, strict validation, refinement contracts, identity hashing, cross-instance references, first-class mixins, introspection, and declarative methods", built on gen-merge (a byte-mode replacement for `lib.evalModules` + `lib.types`), zero nixpkgs.lib (`gen-schema` README). Two layers: **kinds** (schema-level types — open deferred modules that *any* module, including downstream flake inputs, can extend) and **instances** (concrete values materialized by `mkInstanceRegistry`).

What it checks (verified in source):

1. **Instances against their kind's schema — strict by default.** `lib/strict.nix` sets the kind's `_module.freeformType` to a type whose merge always throws, turning the module system's open (freeform) default into a closed record: undeclared keys error immediately, every one named at its path, each with a fix suggestion that parses as written (`STRICT MODE: "addrr" is not declared on host … Fix: schema.host.options.addrr = mkOption { … };`). Opt-out per-kind or via `mkSchemaOption { strict = false }`.

2. **Cross-instance references.** `lib/ref.nix`: `declarationOf "host"` (deferred, bound at registry time via `refs.host`) or `declarationOf <registry>` (direct). Accepts string keys *or* instance values; a value is admitted only if it is the registry member itself — `isCanonicalOf` checks the member's `id_hash` stamp **and** its identity-key values (so `igloo // { addr = "evil" }` and same-named members of other registries are refused by name). Unbound deferred refs refuse by name; refs work under `nullOr`/`listOf`/`setOf`/`attrsOf`/`lazyAttrsOf`/`refined` wrappers; `setOf` dedups by `id_hash`.

3. **Stable identity where Nix `==` cannot be trusted.** `lib/id-hash.nix`: Nix `==` on module-system values can diverge or infinitely recurse, so each instance gets `id_hash = "<kind>:" + sha256(primitive identity keys ++ the kind's minted identity)`. Keys are reflected over the kind's primitive options (str/int/bool/float, both gen-types' and nixpkgs' spellings) with an `identity = false` opt-out or explicit `_identity.keys` (validated against the closed set); `identityHashForKind` recomputes it for kind discovery. This is what `setOf`/`toSet` dedup and membership ride on.

4. **Refinement contracts and validators, co-located with the kind.** `lib/validate.nix`: `mkValidator`/`mkFieldValidator` are `{name, pred/check, message}` records bound to the kind that fire on *every* registry (`validateInstances` → Either, `defaultOnError` throws a formatted list).

Gaps it fills in plain Nix typing: open, cross-module-extendable record types (nixpkgs submodules are closed at their declaration site); typo catching with actionable fixes at the instance boundary; identity-based comparison/dedup where `==` is unreliable; typed reference resolution with membership checks.

## How they split

gen-types is the **leaf checking half**: it verifies that *values* satisfy *types* and that *types* are what their construction says they are. gen-schema is the **registry half** on top of gen-merge: it checks that *instances* satisfy their *kind* (strict keys, refs, refinements, validators) and stamps the stable identity gen-types' minting supplies (`_identity` enters the digest as the kind's `__mint.minted`). gen-merge is the merge engine in between that gen-schema's README calls out as "REPLACES lib.evalModules + lib.types".

Sources: `sini/gen-types` @ `ca90fb1` (README; `lib/checkers.nix`, `lib/refined.nix`, `default.nix`), `sini/gen-schema` @ `cfcad0b` (README; `lib/strict.nix`, `lib/id-hash.nix`, `lib/ref.nix`, `lib/validate.nix`, `default.nix`), both at `main` as of 2026-10-16.","confidence":0.8,"gaps":["eval and clone were both refused in this thread, so no claim was evaluated live — everything rests on README + source-file reads over raw.githubusercontent.com","gen-types lib/strict.nix, lib/validate.nix and lib/default.nix were not read; gen-types' strict/validator/export claims rest on its README","gen-schema lib/instance.nix (registry injection), lib/refined.nix and lib/mixin.nix were not read; the gen-schema README truncated at 1MB (API Reference / Architecture / Theoretical Foundations sections not seen)"],"escalate_forced":"no"}

Accepts string keys *or* instance values; a value is admitted only if it is the registry member itself — `isCanonicalOf` checks the member's `id_hash` stamp **and** its identity-key values (so `igloo // { addr = "evil" }` and same-named members of other registries are refused by name). Unbound deferred refs refuse by name; refs work under `nullOr`/`listOf`/`setOf`/`attrsOf`/`lazyAttrsOf`/`refined` wrappers; `setOf` dedups by `id_hash`.

3. **Stable identity where Nix `==` cannot be trusted.** `lib/id-hash.nix`: Nix `==` on module-system values can diverge or infinitely recurse, so each instance gets `id_hash = "<kind>:" + sha256(primitive identity keys ++ the kind's minted identity)`. questions.question: An aspect does `{ host, ... }: lib.optionalAttrs (host ? gpu) { ... }`. Who sets `host.gpu`, and where?

function.name: reply

draft.answer:
**Nobody in den sets `gpu` — it's yours.** `gpu` is not a built-in host field, and the `host` an aspect receives is exactly your host definition plus your schema tier. There are exactly two places it can come from:

**1. Your host definition (freeform attribute) — the usual route**

The `host` context arg is the resolved *instance* of your `den.hosts.<system>.<name>` declaration (flat `den.hosts.<name>` declarations are normalized into that two-level form by `preprocessHosts` in `nix/lib/entities/_types.nix`). The binding is: `_types.nix` → `resolvedCtxModule` sets `config.resolved = den.lib.resolveEntity kind (ctx // { host = config })`, and `nix/lib/resolve-entity.nix` picks up `entity = ctx.host` — i.e. your own attrset, passed through.

Host instances are built by `hostType` in `nix/lib/entities/host.nix` as `den.lib.schema.mkInstanceType { strict = den.schema.host.isStrict; ... } den.schema.host`, and the only built-in options declared there are `hostName`, `system`, `class`, `aspect`, `description`, `users`, `instantiate`, `intoAttr` plus internal `resolved`/`id_hash`/`__*` keys. No `gpu`.

Because `den.schema.host.isStrict` defaults to `false` (`modules/options.nix`, `isStrict = { default = false }` in the `mkSchemaOption` collections) and gen-schema instances inherit their kind's open/freeform setting (sini/gen-schema README: strict kinds refuse undeclared keys, non-strict kinds accept them), any extra key you put on the instance survives into `host`:

```nix
den.hosts.x86_64-linux.igloo = {
  gpu = "nvidia";
};
```

Den's docs describe this verbatim in `docs/src/content/docs/explanation/entities.mdx` ("Freeform attributes") with an example nearly identical to your aspect: `den.aspects.igloo.includes = [ ({ host, ... }: lib.optionalAttrs (host ? gpu) { nixos.hardware.nvidia.enable = true; }) ]`.

**2. The schema tier, if it should exist on every host**

`den.schema.host` (merged into every host instance via `mkInstanceType ... den.schema.host`, and `den.schema.conf` for all kinds). If you declared it there — e.g. `den.schema.host = { options.gpu = lib.mkOption { default = null; }; }` — every host carries it with a default. The same docs page recommends the schema for "attributes that should exist on every entity of a kind with a default value", since that gives you type checking and documentation.

**One caveat:** if your flake enables strict mode (`imports = [ inputs.den.flakeModules.strict ]`, equivalently `den.schema.host = den.lib.strict` / `isStrict = true`), freeform `gpu` on a host instance is refused with an error naming the key — then route (2) via `den.schema.host` is the only way, and if your aspect currently works, strict mode is not on for the `host` kind.

So: to find who sets it, grep your flake for `gpu` — it will be in a `den.hosts.<…>` definition (route 1) or in a `den.schema.host` entry (route 2).

questions.question: How deep can den aspects nest, and does including `den.aspects.foo._` include grandchildren and foo's own class keys too?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**Nesting depth** — two regimes, one hard cap:

- **Parametric (context-driven) aspects** (`{ host, ... }: ...` style, re-resolved per scope): hard limit of **10 levels**. `maxParametricDepth = 10` in `nix/lib/aspects/fx/aspect.nix`; each re-entry bumps `__parametricDepth`, and `handlers/compile-parametric.nix` throws `den: parametric resolution exceeded 10 levels for '<name>'` once it's `>= 10`.
- **Structural nesting** (nested aspect keys, `provides`/`_` namespaces): **no numeric cap in the source**. Each level is just a lazy module-system type merge — `annotateChildren` in `nix/lib/aspects/types.nix` recurses over attrsets lazily (non-attrset values are never forced), and `compile-static`/`resolve-children` are effect handlers with no depth counter. Depth is bounded only by Nix's eval resources (memory/time), not a den constant. The docs' "deeply nested providers" example is `foo._.bar._.baz` (3 levels, `meta.aspect-chain = ["foo" "bar"]`), but nothing stops you going deeper.

**What `den.aspects.foo._` includes** — neither grandchildren nor foo's own class keys. From `mkUnderscore` in `nix/lib/aspects/types.nix`:

questions.question: I wrote `den.aspects.disk = { device, name ? "main", ... }: { ... }` and included it twice with different devices, but only the first disk is mounted. A positional version `device: { ... }` works. Is this a bug?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Expected behaviour, not a bug — it's exactly den issue #726 (closed by the maintainer, who checked the behaviour against den main f1a3f99), and I confirmed the mechanism in den's source.

Why the named form collapses:
- `{ device, name ? "main", ... }: ...` makes a *parametric* aspect. Calling `den.aspects.disk { device = ...; }` runs the aspect's `__functor` (`resolveAspectWith`, nix/lib/aspects/types.nix), which binds your values as `__scopeHandlers` on a *copy of the same aspect* — it keeps `name = "disk"` and its provenance chain.
- den dedups includes by identity: `check-dedup` (nix/lib/aspects/fx/handlers/check-dedup.nix) keys `includeSeen` per scope on `identity.key` (nix/lib/aspects/fx/identity.nix = provider chain + name, plus a `{ctxId}` suffix only for entity fan-out), first-occurrence-wins. The bound `device` values are not part of that key, so your second call has the same key (`…/disk`) in the same host scope and is gated out — its subtree (the second mount) is never emitted.

Why the positional form works:
`device: { ... }` is not parametric; each call is an ordinary function call returning a fresh *anonymous* aspect (`<anon>`). `check-dedup` only dedups names that are `isMeaningfulName` and not `isSyntheticName` (nix/lib/aspects/types.nix) — anonymous names get a null dedup key and are never deduped, so both instances survive.

Recommended structure (the pattern den's own batteries use, e.g. `den.batteries.tty-autologin`): bake the varying value into the aspect name via `__functor` so each instance has its own identity:

```nix
den.aspects.disk.__functor = _self: cfg:
  { name = "disk(${cfg.name or "main"})"; } // mkDisk cfg;

# callers unchanged:
includes = [ (den.aspects.disk { name = "data"; device = ...; }) ];
```

Distinct names are now distinct aspects (both disks mount); an identical repeated call is still deduped; and you can drop one instance with `excludes = [ (den.aspects.disk { name = "data"; ... }) ]`. If you'd rather not use `__functor`, the positional form `den.aspects.disk = cfg: { ... } // mkDisk cfg;` behaves the same way.

Rule of thumb (from the maintainer on #726): use named args when the aspect should receive context *from den* (`{ host, ... }: ...`); use a positional/plain factory function when *you* supply the arguments.","confidence":0.85,"gaps":["Did not eval the asker's exact flake at their rev — mechanism verified from den main source (check-dedup.nix, identity.nix, types.nix resolveAspectWith) plus closed issue #726","The __functor name-baking fix was verified by the maintainer against den main f1a3f99 per issue #726, not independently eval'd here against the asker's rev"],"escalate_forced":"no"}

questions.question: After updating den, putting an aspect reference in `den.schema.host.excludes` either causes infinite recursion or is ignored. What happened and what is the workaround?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"This is a known den bug with a one-line-fix: **den issue #719**, fixed in **PR #720 (commit `05619dc`, merged 2026-10-13)**.

## What happened

Your update crossed **#717** (`dd59a4c`, 2026-10-12, "migrate to gen-schema's options-first API"), part of the migration of `den.schema` onto gen-schema (#680, 2026-09-15). Since #717, gen-schema mints a kind's **identity** from the contents of its schema collections when an instance is imported. `den.schema.host.excludes` holds aspect references, and an aspect reference can reach *back* into the host being built — e.g. a bracket ref like `<gui/sketchybar>` forces `den.aspects`, and `den.aspects` is built from `den.hosts`. Hashing the collection therefore forces the host during its own import:

- in the simple shape → the exclusion is **silently ignored** (the excluded aspect still applies);
- with nested/bracket refs → **`infinite recursion encountered`**, so every flake output fails to evaluate.

That matches issue #719 exactly ("aspect ref in `den.schema.host.excludes` ignored / infinite recursion since #717"), which includes a failing denTest on `dd59a4c` and the `--show-trace` loop: `den.aspects` → host instance type → gen-schema `stampOk` → canonical encoding of the `den.schema.host` value (incl. its `excludes`) → forcing the excludes element → `den.aspects` → loop.

## The fix (what to do)

**Update den past `05619dc`.** The fix declares `includes` and `excludes` with **`identity = false`** in `modules/options.nix`, so gen-schema keeps those collections out of the kind identity (they are policy *over* aspects, not part of the kind's shape), and it moves the gen pin to the hub rev carrying gen-schema `10f4d12`, which supports `identity = false`. It ships with a 5-cell regression suite (`templates/ci/modules/deadbugs/issue-719-schema-excludes-aspect-ref.nix`) covering direct, bracket and nested-bracket refs in `den.schema.host.excludes`, plus `conf`-tier refs.

One catch: `nix/lib/schema.nix` prefers a **consumer-provided `gen` input** over den's own pinned lock. If your flake declares its own `gen` input and it's older than gen-schema `10f4d12`, the `identity = false` key isn't supported and the recursion comes back — check with `nix flake update gen`.

## Workaround (if you can't update)

Move the exclusion from the schema tier to the **instance tier**:

```nix
den.hosts.x86_64-linux.igloo.excludes = [ <gui/sketchybar> ]; # was: den.schema.host.excludes
```

## What happened

Your update crossed **#717** (`dd59a4c`, 2026-10-12, "migrate to gen-schema's options-first API"), part of the migration of `den.schema` onto gen-schema (#680, 2026-09-15). Since #717, gen-schema mints a kind's **identity** from the contents of its schema collections when an instance is imported. `den.schema.host.excludes` holds aspect references, and an aspect reference can reach *back* into the host being built — e.g. a bracket ref like `<gui/sketchybar>` forces `den.aspects`, and `den.aspects` is built from `den.hosts`. Hashing the collection therefore forces the host during its own import:

- in the simple shape → the exclusion is **silently ignored** (the excluded aspect still applies);
- with nested/bracket refs → **`infinite recursion encountered`**, so every flake output fails to evaluate.

questions.question: On a standalone `user@host` home, den's `inputs'` battery errors that the module argument `inputs'` is defined twice. Why?

function.name: reply

draft.answer:
**Because a standalone `user@host` home is *both* a home and a user in den's scope model, and the `inputs'` battery has parts for both — and on every released rev up to v0.19.0 each part wrote the same module argument directly.**

## The mechanism

The battery (`modules/aspects/batteries/flake-parts/inputs.nix`) is contextual — it has three parts, each firing where its context args exist:

- `osAspect` — `{ host }`, sets the arg on `host.class` (guarded by `host ? class`, so inert for a synthetic classless host)
- `userAspect` — `{ user, host }`, sets the arg on **each of `user.classes`** (e.g. `homeManager`)
- `hmAspect` — `{ home }`, sets the arg on `home.class` (e.g. `homeManager`)

Up through **v0.19.0**, `mkAspect` did this:

```nix
withSystem system ({ inputs', ... }: {
  ${class}._module.args.inputs' = inputs';   # two modules, same key → conflict
});
```

A home named `user@host` (with the host *not* declared in `den.hosts`) gets, from `nix/lib/entities/home.nix` (synthesized in #605, v0.18.0):

- `config._module.args.host` = a minimal synthesized `{ name = hostName; system }`
- `config._module.args.user` = a bound user with `classes = [ config.class ]` — i.e. `[ "homeManager" ]`

So inside the home's own scope, **both** `userAspect` (via the bound user, whose only class is `homeManager`) and `hmAspect` (via `home.class = "homeManager"`) fire, and both land in the same `homeConfigurations."user@host"` module tree, each writing `homeManager._module.args.inputs'`. `_module.args` is just an option of the target module system (nixpkgs `lib/modules.nix`); when two modules in one tree define the same key, the system rejects it — the "The module argument `inputs'` is defined twice" error.

A plain `den.homes.<system>.tux` home doesn't hit this: it has no `host` in scope, so `userAspect` (which destructures `{ user, host }`) never fires — only `hmAspect` does.

## The fix (already on main, not in a release)

Commit **f1d16b1** — *"fix: inputs' and self' batteries define their module argument once on a user@host home (#721) (#722)"*, 2026-10-14, i.e. **after v0.19.0** (2026-09-24). Both `inputs'` and `self'` now add a single keyed module to the class:

```nix
${class}.imports = [
  {
    key = "den.batteries.inputs'/${system}";
    _module.args.inputs' = inputs';
  }
];
```

The module system deduplicates imports by `key` (`lib/modules.nix` `filterModules`: "the final list of unique-by-key modules"), so no matter how many of the battery's parts match, exactly one copy of the arg-setting module survives. The same commit adds a deadbugs regression test, `templates/ci/modules/deadbugs/standalone-qualified-home-inputs.nix`, which reproduces exactly your case (`den.homes.x86_64-linux."tux@igloo"`, host undeclared, `den.batteries.inputs'` included, home using `{ inputs', ... }`) plus a control for plain `tux`.

## What to do

- **Update to a den rev containing f1d16b1** (main, after v0.19.0). If you're pinned to v0.19.0 you're affected; `self'` has the identical bug and was fixed in the same commit.
- Note that including the battery per-aspect (`den.aspects."user@host".includes = [ den.batteries.inputs' ]`) does **not** avoid it — both parts fire inside the home's own scope, which is why the deadbugs test used that form. On a pre-fix rev your options are to skip `inputs'`/`self'` for that home and reach the flake inputs another way (e.g. the `flake-scope` battery, documented as the non-flake-parts counterpart of `inputs'`/`self'`, or supplying the arg yourself in the home's module tree).

questions.question: With flake-file writing npins pins for a flakeless den setup, my `follows` declarations are lost and the top-level nixpkgs-lib input is missing. Why, and what fixes it?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Both symptoms come from one design decision in flake-file's pins writer (`denful/flake-file`, `modules/pins/default.nix` + `queue.bash`): **a pin file can only store fetches, not `follows`**.

**Why `follows` is "lost":**
- `collectFollowing` gathers every input that sets `follows` at *any* nesting level. The comment: *"such an input is never fetched under its own name, so it needs no pin."* Those names become `skipSet`; `queue.bash` pre-marks them `SEEN` so they are never pinned, and the final prune loop deletes any pre-existing pin of those names. `npins/sources.json` (flat name→repo/rev/hash) simply cannot represent a follow.
- The writer compensates by writing the follows into a sidecar next to the lock: `npins/follows.nix`, with the comment: *"The follows declared there, for with-inputs: pass this file as (or with) its overrides."*
- In the flakeless den template (`denful/den`, `templates/noflake/default.nix`) the wiring is `import sources.with-inputs sources { /* only an optional local-checkout override */ }` — **nothing passes `follows.nix` to `with-inputs`**, so at resolution time your follows don't apply. (The generated `inputs.nix` from `write-inputs` *does* keep follows — `inputsExpr` preserves string follows — so it's the lock/resolution side where they vanish.)

**Why the top-level `nixpkgs-lib` is missing:**
If your declaration is `nixpkgs-lib.follows = …` (e.g. `"nixpkgs"` to dedupe), that input is in `skipSet` and has no URL of its own, so it never gets a pin — and nothing re-discovers it (den's own `flake.nix` is `{ outputs = _: import ./nix; }` with no `inputs`, so the transitive discovery in `queue.bash` finds nothing for den). The pin is pruned → no top-level `nixpkgs-lib` in `sources.json` → `with-inputs` has nothing to auto-follow by name, and per its README an unresolvable follow target becomes `null` and the dependent outputs call is skipped.
Note the contrast the module spells out: *"a declared top-level input keeps its pin even when a nested input of the same name follows something."* The pin survives if `nixpkgs-lib` is declared with its own `url` and only the *nested* copy carries the follows.

**Fix A (keep your dedupe) — feed the sidecar into `with-inputs`:**
```nix
let
  sources = import ./npins;
  with-inputs = import sources.with-inputs sources (import ./npins/follows.nix);
  outputs = inputs: (inputs.nixpkgs.lib.evalModules { ... }).config;
in
with-inputs outputs
```
`follows.nix` is exactly "the follows declared there, and nothing else", which is the spec shape `with-inputs` expects (`b.follows = "a"` aliases to `allInputs.a`; `follows = ""` disconnects). **Fix B (make `nixpkgs-lib` a real pinned input):**
```nix

  nixpkgs-lib.url = "github:NixOS/nixpkgs-lib";    # pinnable → stays in sources.json
  den.url = "github:denful/den";
  den.inputs.nixpkgs-lib.follows = "nixpkgs-lib";  # nested follows → stays in follows.nix
};
```

questions.question: In den, when should a custom class be forwarded into an existing class and when should it be evaluated on its own?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"## When to forward vs. evaluate a custom class in den

The decision axis is: **does an existing class/module system already have a place where your content belongs, and should that system do the evaluation?**

### Forward into an existing class — when your content is *options of an existing module system*

Use `den.batteries.forward` (or lower-level: register `den.classes.<name>` + a `den.lib.policy.route`/`deliver` policy) when the class is a **view over an existing class** — its content gets collected and nested into a submodule path of a target class, and is evaluated as part of that target's single module-system run. This is exactly how den implements its own integrations:

- `user` → `users.users.<name>` on the host's OS class
- `homeManager` → `home-manager.users.<name>` (plus importing the HM OS module, `osConfig` arg)
- `hjem` → `hjem.users.<name>`, `maid` → `users.users.<name>.maid`
- Example custom class from the guide: `container` → `virtualisation.oci-containers.containers.<name>`

Forwarding is the right tool when you want:
- an **alias / shorthand** (`hm` → `homeManager`; `user` instead of `nixos.users.users.alice`),
- **fan-out to several classes** from one key (the built-in `os` class lands in both `nixos` and `darwin`; the community `nix` class lands in `nixos` + `homeManager`),
- **guarded routing** (the `persys` example forwards into `environment.persistence.<dir>` only when the host imported the impermanence module; the `hmLinux`/`hmDarwin` example guards on `pkgs.stdenv`),
- separation of concerns inside one big module hierarchy, with one place holding the `guard`/`adaptArgs` logic.

Rule of thumb: if the target class has an option path that can own your content, forward — the existing system stays the single source of truth and does the evaluation for you.

### Evaluate on its own — when the content has *no existing class to live in* and needs its own evaluation/output

Give the class its own module evaluation and its own output when:
- the content is **not NixOS/Darwin/HM options** at all (e.g. terraform/terranix-style structured config) — collect the class bucket and instantiate it yourself with `den.lib.policy.instantiate`:
  ```nix
  policy.instantiate {
    name = "${host.name}-tf";
    class = "terranix";
    instantiate = { modules, ... }: modules;  # how to build from collected modules
    intoAttr = [ "terranixModules" host.name ];
  };
  ```
  (the "terranix pattern" from the policies reference),
- the class needs **its own system/config as a separate build**: standalone home-manager homes, the MicroVM template's *runnable* VMs, or a guest VM resolved as an **isolated host pipeline** whose result is its own `nixosConfiguration`.

### The two combine — and the real question is "who evaluates, and where does it land?"

The MicroVM template shows the hybrid: each guest is *evaluated on its own* (isolated host pipeline, "its modules stay external"), then the resolved modules are **delivered into the existing server class** at `microvm.vms.<name>.config` via `policy.provide`. When the delivery target *re-instantiates* the modules in its own evaluation (e.g. the microvm guest config), use `mode = "verbatim"` on `deliver`/`route` so the collected module wrappers are placed by reference and the target sees them live alongside its base modules.

### Sources
- `docs/src/content/docs/guides/custom-classes.mdx` — `forward` battery, `den.classes` fields (`forwardTo`, `parentPath`, `parentArg`), `guard`/`adaptArgs`/`adapterModule`
- `docs/src/content/docs/guides/custom-class-examples.mdx` — alias, platform, role, guarded examples
- `docs/src/content/docs/reference/policies.mdx` — `policy.deliver`/`route`/`provide`/`instantiate` specs (incl. `verbatim` for microvm)

## When to forward vs. evaluate a custom class in den

The decision axis is: **does an existing class/module system already have a place where your content belongs, and should that system do the evaluation?**

### Forward into an existing class — when your content is *options of an existing module system*

Use `den.batteries.forward` (or lower-level: register `den.classes.<name>` + a `den.lib.policy.route`/`deliver` policy) when the class is a **view over an existing class** — its content gets collected and nested into a submodule path of a target class, and is evaluated as part of that target's single module-system run. This is exactly how den implements its own integrations:

- `user` → `users.users.<name>` on the host's OS class
- `homeManager` → `home-manager.users.<name>` (plus importing the HM OS module, `osConfig` arg)
- `hjem` → `hjem.users.<name>`, `maid` → `users.users.<name>.maid`
- Example custom class from the guide: `container` → `virtualisation.oci-containers.containers.<name>`

Forwarding is the right tool when you want:
- an **alias / shorthand** (`hm` → `homeManager`; `user` instead of `nixos.users.users.alice`),
- **fan-out to several classes** from one key (the built-in `os` class lands in both `nixos` and `darwin`; the community `nix` class lands in `nixos` + `homeManager`),
- **guarded routing** (the `persys` example forwards into `environment.persistence.<dir>` only when the host imported the impermanence module; the `hmLinux`/`hmDarwin` example guards on `pkgs.stdenv`),
- separation of concerns inside one big module hierarchy, with one place holding the `guard`/`adaptArgs` logic.

Rule of thumb: if the target class has an option path that can own your content, forward — the existing system stays the single source of truth and does the evaluation for you.

### Evaluate on its own — when the content has *no existing class to live in* and needs its own evaluation/output

Give the class its own module evaluation and its own output when:
- the content is **not NixOS/Darwin/HM options** at all (e.g. terraform/terranix-style structured config) — collect the class bucket and instantiate it yourself with `den.lib.policy.instantiate`:
  ```nix
  policy.instantiate {
    name = "${host.name}-tf";
    class = "terranix";
    instantiate = { modules, ... }: modules;  # how to build from collected modules
    intoAttr = [ "terranixModules" host.name ];
  };
  ```
  (the "terranix pattern" from the policies reference),
- the class needs **its own system/config as a separate build**: standalone home-manager homes, the MicroVM template's *runnable* VMs, or a guest VM resolved as an **isolated host pipeline** whose result is its own `nixosConfiguration`.

### The two combine — and the real question is "who evaluates, and where does it land?"

The MicroVM template shows the hybrid: each guest is *evaluated on its own* (isolated host pipeline, "its modules stay external"), then the resolved modules are **delivered into the existing server class** at `microvm.vms.<name>.config` via `policy.provide`. When the delivery target *re-instantiates* the modules in its own evaluation (e.g. the microvm guest config), use `mode = "verbatim"` on `deliver`/`route` so the collected module wrappers are placed by reference and the target sees them live alongside its base modules.

questions.question: How do I apply an overlay from another flake (for example a rust overlay) to every host in a den config?

function.name: reply

draft.answer:
In den, a host's package set is built by its own OS-class `nixpkgs` module, so the overlay goes in `nixpkgs.overlays` inside an aspect — and you make it apply to **every host** by including that aspect in the host schema:

```nix
{ den, inputs, ... }:
{
  den.aspects.my-overlays.os.nixpkgs.overlays = [
    inputs.rust-overlay.overlays.default
    # plus any local overlays: (final: prev: { … })
  ];

  # every host includes this aspect, so the overlay applies fleet-wide
  den.schema.host.includes = [ den.aspects.my-overlays ];
}
```

Details from den's docs (`docs/src/content/docs/guides/nixpkgs.mdx` on `main`) and source:

- **`os` is the cross-platform key.** It forwards into both `nixos` and `darwin`. Verified in `modules/aspects/batteries/os-class.nix`: the built-in `den.policies.os-to-host` (auto-included via `den.default`) routes `os` content to `host.class` for any host whose class is `nixos` or `darwin`.
- **Prefer `den.schema.host.includes` over `den.default.includes`** for a host-level setting: `den.default` also reaches every user and home, so it's wider than you need.
- **Pitfall:** a flake-parts `perSystem._module.args.pkgs = import inputs.nixpkgs { overlays = …; }` only affects flake outputs (packages, devShells, checks) — den hosts are instantiated with their modules only, so that `pkgs` never reaches them. Host overlays must go through `nixpkgs.overlays` as above.
- **If the overlay should travel with the feature** (delete the aspect → overlay disappears), use the quirk recipe from the same page: each aspect contributes under a `nixpkgs-overlays` quirk, and one consumer aspect applies the collected list to `nixpkgs.overlays` per class. Note the quirk must wrap the overlay: `nixpkgs-overlays = _: [ inputs.rust-overlay.overlays.default ];` — an unwrapped function-valued quirk gets called with the context and breaks evaluation.
- **Home Manager:** with the default (each home builds its own `pkgs`), an overlay only needed for home packages must also be set in the `homeManager` class; under `home-manager.useGlobalPkgs = true` homes reuse the host's `pkgs`, so the host-side overlay covers them.
- den's own fleet example uses **fenix** (`inputs.fenix.overlays.default`) as the rust overlay — worth considering over `rust-overlay` if you want what den's tested setups use.

Caveat: I read this from den's `main` docs/source (clone was unavailable in this thread, so via raw fetches); I couldn't evaluate your specific flake since no repo/rev was given, so I haven't verified it against your exact den version.

questions.question: I wrote `options = lib.mkMerge [ (myOptions lib) ];` in a module. It half works, but forcing the whole option tree fails with an option declaration named `contents` that has type list. Why?

{"answer":"Because `lib.mkMerge` is **not an attrset merge anymore** — in current nixpkgs it is the module system's *property* constructor, and under `options` that wrapper is misread as an option tree.

What happens, from the nixpkgs source (checked on `master`):

1. `lib.mkMerge` is inherited from `lib.modules` (`lib/default.nix`: `inherit (self.modules) ... mkMerge ...`), and `lib/attrsets.nix` no longer defines the old `foldl (a: b: a // b) {}` version — that operation is now `lib.mergeAttrsList`. The current definition, in `lib/modules.nix`, is:
   ```nix
   mkMerge = contents: { _type = "merge"; inherit contents; };
   ```
   So your line
   ```nix
   options = lib.mkMerge [ (myOptions lib) ];
   ```
   sets your module's `options` to `{ _type = "merge"; contents = [ <your options attrset> ] }` — a *config property wrapper*, not an options tree. (`unifyModuleSyntax` takes `options` verbatim; `pushDownProperties`, which expands `_type = "merge"`, only runs on `config` values, never on `options`.)

2. `mergeModules'` in `lib/modules.nix` then reads that attrset *as the option declaration tree*: your module now "declares" two top-level options — `_type` (the string `"merge"`) and **`contents`**, whose value is the wrapper's `contents` field, i.e. a **list**. When the merge recurses into that subtree it hits:
   ```nix

     throw ''
       An option declaration for `${concatStringsSep "." prefix}' has type
       `${typeOf subtree}' rather than an attribute set.
       Did you mean to define this outside of `options'?
     ''
   ```
   → `An option declaration for 'contents' has type 'list' rather than an attribute set.` — the exact failure you describe.

3. Why it "half works": that throw is lazy. The `contents` subtree is only forced when `options.contents` (or the whole `options` tree) is forced. Normal evaluation forces `config`, and the per-subtree `unmatchedDefns` short-circuits with `if configs == [ ] then [ ]` (nothing defines values under `config.contents`), so the bad subtree is never touched — until you force the whole option tree.

Fix: drop the wrapper; with a single element there is nothing to merge:
```nix

```
If you genuinely have several options attrsets to combine, use the attrset merge:
```nix
options = lib.mergeAttrsList [ (myOptions lib) (otherOptions lib) ];
```

questions.question: The den docs show both `provides.to-users` and policies with `policy.include` for cross-entity delivery. Which should I use for new configurations?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**Prefer the policy (`policy.include`) for new configurations** — that's den's own documented guidance, and the two mechanisms are the same thing under the hood anyway.

**Why the docs say this** (from `docs/src/content/docs/explanation/choosing-a-mechanism.mdx`, `denful/den` @ `main`):

> "`provides` is shorter and stays supported. For new configurations prefer the policy: the `git` aspect stays reusable anywhere, and 'who gets it' is visible as a rule instead of buried in one host's aspect."

The contrast the docs draw:

```nix
# provides: the relationship is written inside the behaviour
den.aspects.igloo.provides.to-users.homeManager.programs.git.enable = true;

# policy: the behaviour is a plain aspect, the relationship is a rule
den.aspects.git.homeManager.programs.git.enable = true;
den.policies.git-for-igloo-users = { host, user, ... }:
  lib.optional (host.name == "igloo") (den.lib.policy.include den.aspects.git);
den.schema.user.includes = [ den.policies.git-for-igloo-users ];
```

**They are one mechanism, two placements.** `provides.to-users` isn't a separate delivery engine: `mkCrossPolicy` in `nix/lib/aspects/fx/aspect/provide.nix` (lines 15–38) registers every `provides` key as an aspect-scoped policy effect whose body is literally `[ (policy.include result) ]` (for `to-users`/`to-hosts`). The only difference is *where the relationship lives*: inside the behaviour's aspect (`provides`), or beside it as an activation rule (`den.policies` + `includes`). So the decision is a style/organization one:

- **Use `provides.to-users`** when the relationship is intrinsic to the feature — e.g. the `hyprland` aspect carrying both its NixOS half and its per-user home-manager half (`den.aspects.hyprland.provides.to-users.homeManager.…`). Short, self-contained, and the docs use exactly this pattern.
- **Use a policy** when you want the aspect to stay ignorant of who uses it — reusable anywhere, shareable through namespaces/flakes — and to express "who gets it" as a visible rule (activate via `den.schema.user.includes`, a specific aspect's `includes`, or `den.default.includes`).

**Two foot-guns from the docs worth knowing** (`explanation/where-config-lands.mdx`):

1. A user-named child on the host aspect (`den.aspects.igloo.tux`) does **not** target one user — the built-in `host-to-users` policy (`modules/policies/core.nix`) includes it in *every* user's scope. To reach exactly one user, use `provides.tux` (or a policy matching `user.name == "tux"`).
2. A bare `homeManager` key on a host aspect reaches **nowhere** (no warning) — host→user delivery only happens through an explicit edge: `provides.to-users`, `provides.<user>`, or the `host-aspects` battery (use the latter when each *user* should decide to opt in to the host's home config).

questions.question: My formatter's dead-code linter removed an unused `user` argument from a den class module, and now the module stopped applying. Why does an unused argument matter?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Short version: in den, a class module's argument list is not just a function signature — it is the module's **routing contract** with the context. The linter saw `user` as unused *inside the body*, but den reads the signature via `builtins.functionArgs` and uses it to decide *where* the module applies at all.

**The principle** (den README, denful/den@main): "No mkIf / enable clutter. **The shape of the context is the condition** — a function that asks for `{ host, user }` simply doesn't run where there's no user."

**What the source shows** (all denful/den, `main`):

1. Flat-form class modules (`nixos = { user, config, pkgs, ... }`) are wrapped by `wrapFunctionModule` in `nix/lib/aspects/fx/class-module.nix`: it computes `denArgNames = filter (k: ctx ? k) (attrNames (functionArgs module))`, pre-applies those context values, and advertises only the rest to the module system (`docs/.../explanation/class-modules.mdx`: "The pipeline inspects `builtins.functionArgs`, identifies which args exist in the current context, pre-applies those values…").
2. The **binding rule** (`docs/.../explanation/parametric.mdx`, implemented in `nix/lib/aspects/fx/handlers/bind.nix`): a module that destructures an entity-kind arg (`host`, `user`, `home`, …) is (1) bound once where that kind is in context, (2) **fanned out once per descendant** where it isn't (a host-scope `{ user, … }` module becomes one per-user instance each with a distinct `__ctxId` like `{user=bob}` and `meta.contextDependent = true`, so dedup keeps every user's copy separate), or (3) *inert, silently* where the kind is neither in-context nor a descendant.
3. The reverse of your change is the documented footgun: `class-modules.mdx` — "If your class module isn't taking effect, check whether all its entity args are in context at the scope where it's being resolved." Your case is the mirror image: **removing** `user` moves the module off the per-user path. With no declared entity args it's no longer parametric — `computeModuleIdentity` in `nix/lib/aspects/fx/wrap-classes.nix` strips the `{user=…}` identity suffix (`stripCtxSuffix`, `nix/lib/aspects/fx/identity.nix`) for non-context-dependent modules, all per-user instances collapse to one shared `_file` identity, and the module system dedups them. So it's no longer applied *per user* — it either applies once at the emitting scope where you weren't looking, or (depending on your class, e.g. a purely per-user class) it appears to have stopped applying entirely.

**What to do:**

- If the module is meant to be **per-user**: put `user` back in the signature and mark it for the linter (an allowlist/exception or a comment annotation on that parameter). Two traps: the name must be exactly `user` — `_user` is a different name and won't match the entity kind — and give it **no default**: a defaulted arg is optional, and only non-default (required) args are probed for fan-out.
- If the module genuinely is **host-scoped** and the linter was right: the removal was still a semantic change, not a no-op — check where its config now lands (once, at the emitting scope) rather than assuming it vanished.

questions.question: My existing flake is large. Can I migrate to den gradually, keeping my current nixosConfigurations and modules while moving pieces over?

function.name: reply

{"answer":"Yes — den is built for exactly this. Its official "From Flake to Den" guide (den.denful.dev/guides/from-flake-to-den) describes an incremental path that keeps your current flake working while you move pieces over:

1. Add `inputs.den.url = "github:denful/den"` and `inputs.import-tree.url = "github:denful/import-tree"` to your existing flake; nothing else changes.
2. Create `modules/den.nix` starting with `imports = [ inputs.den.flakeModule ];` and declare the hosts/users/aspects for the first pieces you move.
3. In your existing flake, evaluate the den part in isolation:
   `den = (inputs.nixpkgs.lib.evalModules { modules = [ (inputs.import-tree ./modules) ]; specialArgs.inputs = inputs; }).config;`
   then `inherit (den.den.hosts.x86_64-linux) igloo;`
4. Keep your current system as-is and just append the generated module:
   `nixosConfigurations.igloo = nixosSystem { modules = [ <all your current NixOS modules> igloo.mainModule ]; };`
   Same pattern for darwinConfigurations (`iceberg.mainModule`).
5. If you use flake-parts, add `inputs.den.flakeOutputs.flake` to that same `modules = [ ... ]` list.
6. The `import-tree` battery exists specifically for importing your existing legacy module trees, so current module files can be pulled in without being rewritten one by one.

questions.question: Does `lib.recursiveUpdate` concatenate lists that appear on both sides?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"No — `lib.recursiveUpdate` does not concatenate lists that appear on both sides. I checked `lib/attrsets.nix` in current nixpkgs `master` (via the raw GitHub URL; `clone`/`eval` were unavailable in this run), and both the docs and the code agree:

```nix
  /**
    A recursive variant of the update operator `//`.  The recursion
    stops when one of the attribute values is not an attribute set,
    in which case the right hand side value takes precedence over the
    left hand side value.
  */
  recursiveUpdate =
    lhs: rhs:
    recursiveUpdateUntil (
      path: lhs: rhs:
      !(isAttrs lhs && isAttrs rhs)
    ) lhs rhs;
```

Recursion continues only while **both** sides are attribute sets. When one side is not an attrset — including the case where *both* sides are lists — recursion stops and the **second argument's value wins, wholesale**. There is no `++`/`concatLists` in the implementation:

```nix
lib.recursiveUpdate { x = [ "a" "b" ]; } { x = [ "c" ]; }
# => { x = [ "c" ]; }   # right-hand list replaces; left list dropped
```

If you need list concatenation on collisions, that's a different combinator: `lib.zipAttrsWith` / `lib.foldAttrs` collect colliding values into lists, and NixOS's options machinery concatenates list options across definitions. `recursiveUpdate` is deliberately the "deep replace" operator, with the same precedence direction as `//` (second argument wins) applied recursively.","confidence":0.9,"gaps":["Eval runner and clone were unavailable in this evaluation run, so the behavior was verified by reading nixpkgs master source (raw.githubusercontent.com) rather than a live eval of a concrete expression."],"escalate_forced":"no"}

questions.question: `builtins.toJSON config` fails on my module config. What does the error say and what is the usual cause?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**What the error says**

`builtins.toJSON` only knows how to serialize strings, integers, floats, booleans, null, lists, sets, paths and derivations — per the Nix 2.34.9 manual, sets (except derivations) become JSON objects, derivations become the string of their output path, and paths are copied to the store and rendered as that store path. Anything else makes it abort. The classic failure on a module config is the unserializable-**function** error, roughly:

```
error: cannot serialize the function … to JSON
```

Two important version notes:

- On **older Nix** (pre-2.12 era), hitting a function during `toJSON` is a hard error of the shape above.
- On **modern Nix**, functions no longer fail: they serialize silently as the string `"undefined"`. So if you're on a recent Nix and it *still* fails, the culprit is something else (e.g. an external value), and if it "succeeds", check the output for `"undefined"` entries — those are functions that got dropped.

**The usual cause**

Your `config` contains values of function type. For a final NixOS-style module config (which is what a den aspect projects to the `nixos` class), the usual suspects are:

- `nixpkgs.overlays` — a list of lambdas (`{ pkgs, … }: …`),
- `config.nixpkgs.pkgs` if it's present in the config — a package set full of functions (`callPackage`, `stdenv.mkDerivation`, …),
- options of `raw`/function type you set to lambdas,
- in den specifically, pipeline wrapper markers such as `__fn` / `__args` (parametric wrappers), `__contentValues`, `__scopeHandlers` if they survive into the projected config — den's own debugging docs list these as the structural markers in the pipeline.

**How to find the offender**

```nix
builtins.map (a: { attr = a; type = builtins.typeOf config.${a}; }) (builtins.attrNames config)
```

then drill into the attrs whose type is `lambda` (or `set` if you suspect an embedded package set / wrapper attrset).

**What to do about it**

- If you're on old Nix: upgrade; on current Nix the same config evaluates (functions become `"undefined"`).
- Serialize a projection instead of the whole config: `builtins.toJSON (lib.removeAttrs config [ "nixpkgs" … ])` or just the keys you care about.
- If den wrapper attrs (`__fn`, `__args`, …) are leaking into your projected config, that's a den bug/behavior worth reporting — I couldn't check den's source in this thread (see gaps).

questions.question: Why does `1 / 2` evaluate to 0 in Nix?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Because `1` and `2` are both **integers**, and Nix is typed about numbers: integers are 64-bit, floats are 64-bit IEEE-754 doubles, and the `/` operator follows its operands' types.

In the Nix source (2.20.4, `src/libexpr/primops.cc`, `prim_div` — the primop the parser desugares `/` into as `__div`):

- if **either** operand is a float → `v.mkFloat(...)`, a real float division
- if **both** are integers → `v.mkInt(i1 / i2)`, plain C integer division, which **truncates toward zero**

So `1 / 2` is integer division: `1 / 2 == 0` (as in C). Same for `7 / 2 == 3`.

To get a float result, make at least one operand a float:

```nix
1.0 / 2   # → 0.5
```

One more quirk from the same function: division by zero is an evaluation error, and `minInt / -1` (i.e. `minInt / -1`) is rejected as an overflow.

Source: https://github.com/NixOS/nix/blob/2.20.4/src/libexpr/primops.cc (`prim_div`, "Integer arithmetic" section).","confidence":0.9,"gaps":["Did not run an eval against a specific repo/rev (the question carried none); verified by reading Nix 2.20.4 source, where prim_div implements int/int as C integer division"],"escalate_forced":"no"}

questions.question: Why does `"x${opt}"` fail when `opt` is null, while `toString null` works?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Because `${...}` is **not** `toString` — it's string concatenation with *strict* type coercion, while `toString` is an explicit *converting* builtin. They both end up in the same internal function, `coerceToString`, but with different settings.

**What I checked** (NixOS/nix @ `master`, `src/libexpr/eval.cc` and `src/libexpr/primops.cc`; matches the Nix 2.35.2 reference manual):

- `"x${opt}"` desugars to string concatenation (`ExprConcatStrings::eval`). - `builtins.toString` (`prim_toString` in `primops.cc`) calls the same `coerceToString` with `coerceMore = true`. That mode converts: `null → ""`, `false → ""`, `true → "1"`, int → decimal string, float → decimal string, list → space-joined strings, string → unchanged. "prefix-${if opt == null then "null" else opt}"  # if you want the literal word "null"

{"answer":"**Why it errors**

A pattern like `{ a ? 1 }` declares the *exact* set of attributes the function accepts. In current Nix, pattern matching is strict: calling it with an attribute that isn't in the pattern throws

```

```

I verified this in Nix's source (NixOS/nix, `master`):

- `src/libexpr/eval.cc`, `EvalState::callFunction`: after binding the formals, it checks `if (!formals->ellipsis && attrsUsed != args[0]->attrs()->size())` and throws `TypeError "function '%1%' called with unexpected argument '%2%'"` for the first attribute not in the pattern.

So `{ a ? 1 }` has `ellipsis = false` → any extra attribute is an error. The nix.dev "Nix language basics" tutorial documents exactly this: "The argument defines the exact attributes that have to be in that set. Leaving out or passing additional attributes is an error."

Add an ellipsis to the pattern:

```nix
f = { a ? 1, ... }: a;
f { b = 2; }  # → 1 (default for a; b is ignored)
```

- If you also want to *use* the extra attributes, bind the whole set with `@`:
  `args@{ a ? 1, ... }: ...` (or `{ a ? 1, ... }@args: ...`)
- Or skip the pattern entirely and use a normal selector with a default, which accepts any set:
  `f = args: args.a or 1;`

**Caveat:** this strictness is recent Nix behavior (documented in the current nix.dev manual; the same error is reported from early 2024, Nix 2.20-era, onward).
